subtopic: TRIBUTES ON RETIREMENT FROM BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON RETIREMENT FROM BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Recently the right hon. gentleman the member for Woodford, Sir Winston Churchill, announced his retirement from the British House of Commons. As the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom said at Westminster this week, this is an occasion both of sadness and of grandeur; sadness, because the greatest parliamentary career of our time is coming to an end; grandeur, because of the honour and lustre which that career has brought to the institution of parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of this house would wish to put on record the unbounded admiration and gratitude of the Canadian House of Commons for Sir Winston's services to freedom and to free men everywhere. We shall remain forever in his debt for the inspiration and the achievements of his life and his work; above all for his leadership in the struggle against what he once described as "the foulest and most soul destroying tyranny which had ever darkened and stained the pages of history."
The sweep of Sir Winston's career across our history is still so close to us that we can only view with awe the part he has played in this turbulent twentieth century. We are so close to him that it is difficult to pay adequate tribute to, or even to keep in any proper perspective, one who always matched, and often dominated, the events of his age.
He is the heroic war leader; the transcendent politician, parliamentarian and statesman; the adventurer, soldier, orator, historian; the most human of human beings; the man who never knew fear, never admitted defeat, never confused victory with peace, never let prejudice confound progress. He was a manysided genius, the Renaissance man 400 years after the Renaissance.
Though our most cherished and most vivid recollection of him is as the war leader, indomitable, vast, inspiring with his voice 20220-390J
alone millions of men around the world, this day, in this chamber, in this daughter of the mother of parliaments, we pay tribute to the man of the House of Commons in which he served as a member for 64 years. He is the last of a great generation of parliamentary leaders whose skill in parliamentary debate was equalled only by his love of it. No house of commons will see his like again.
We recall, Mr. Speaker, with affection the occasion when his presence and the nobility of his spirit enriched this chamber. We are, I am sure, as one today in acknowledging the immeasurable debt that all free men and the parliaments by which they are served owe to this man. So we wish him and Lady Churchill, a fitting helpmate for such a man, further good years ahead to enjoy the esteem and affection of their millions and millions of friends in every corner of the world.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON RETIREMENT FROM BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the right hon. Prime Minister in his tribute to Sir Winston Churchill. We have a double interest, the Prime Minister and I, being members of the imperial privy council, as all privy councillors in Canada have an additional interest in that Sir Winston Churchill is a member of the privy council of our country.
I saw him first almost 48 years ago from the gallery of the House of Commons in Westminster when, following the tribulations of Gallipoli, he was in disgrace. His career, they said, was over. They have said it several times since, and in every case have been wrong. I recall him then, in the uniform of a lieutenant colonel, rising to speak in the British house and that house emptying, as it does when the members desire not to hear the member who is speaking. He was indomitable, courageous, fearless.
I saw him again in the 1930's and again he was the Cassandra of British public men when he foresaw the fear of the shadow of Hitler over Europe. I met him during the early days of war. I said to him "I saw you first when you were in disgrace, Mr. Prime Minister". His reply was "Which time was that?"
He has a sense of humour, a knowledge of history unparalleled in public men. From

Sir Winston Churchill Retirement his earliest days, as the Prime Minister has said, he was a child of the House of Commons. When one goes back to 1896, as his regiment was about to leave for India he recorded these words, "The Churchills peg out early, so I am going to make sure of my innings".
He came into parliament when Sir Wilfrid Laurier had been prime minister for about four years. Queen Victoria was on the throne. He lived through the greatest events in modern history, if not in all history. As the Prime Minister has said, he was orator, warrior, writer, painter; a statesman who has held more positions than any other leader in all the cabinets of the United Kingdom. He is immortal while yet he lives.
In all his greatness, sir, what stands out is that he was always a House of Commons man. His sense of humour, his ability in the thrust and cut of debate, devastating at times, was never wounding. Many examples of his wit are known to members, but the one which particularly appeals to me was in response to an interruption he received from a member whose legs were very short and who from time to time interrupted him. Sir Winston was in the midst of a speech, and his response was "The hon. member should not be so ready to hop down off his perch". That was Churchill. Some of his replies are immortal. None caused more than the temporary disillusionment of those who were the recipients thereof, because he never sought to destroy those with whom he disagreed.
One often hears it said that it must have been wonderful to live in some other age, in the golden ages of the past. We who have lived in the lifetime of Sir Winston Churchill could not ask for more. In the last war, as in the first world war, he was the embodiment of the determination of the British people. When freedom was challenged there were strong men who were filled with fear. One will never forget, as the Prime Minister has said, those words of his during the last war when he took his fellow men from the valley of fear to the heights of Everest. His words are immortal. The music of his language carries a bell tone sincerity cast in the mould of Gibbons and Macaulay. He moved men.
I think of him in a personal sense. I have visited him in his home on several occasions. He is the embodiment of those virtues that have meant so much to Britain's leadership.
The Prime Minister mentioned Lady Churchill. No man can achieve greatness without a wife with the capacity to understand and at the same time be critical in the best
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
sense of the word. Sir Winston has been blessed with such a wife for more than 57 years. She has been his constant companion, his devoted adviser and the inspiration of his life.
We are not here to speak in the manner of a requiem. We are here as Canadians in the parliament of this country, believing in freedom and knowing what Churchill's contribution has been. May he, as the Prime Minister said, continue for whatever time lies ahead to have the knowledge that wherever freedom lives the name of Churchill will also be revered.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON RETIREMENT FROM BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is altogether fitting that this House of Commons should pay tribute to the greatest parliamentarian of our time, Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill. His parliamentary career spans a period of 64 years, with the exception of one short interval of two years. He has occupied his seat in the British House of Commons for the last time. The House of Commons will be a poorer place for his leaving.
However, it is not the length of his service but rather its quality for which he will be remembered for many years with affection and gratitude. Whether as a member of the opposition, a minister of the crown or as prime minister of his country, he brought his great gifts as a parliamentarian and orator to the service of his native land.
History will undoubtedly judge him as the greatest Englishman of this century, and probably one of the greatest of all time. It is astonishing that one man should have crowded so much experience into a single lifetime. It is hard to realize that this man rode with the Lancers at Omdurman; was captured by General Botha in the Boer war; was first lord of the admiralty in world war I and returned to that post at the outbreak of world war II.
However, he will be remembered most for his leadership of Britain and the commonwealth when Hitler's legions were at the gate and we stood almost alone. It was then that his dauntless courage and his matchless oratory came into their own. Someone has said he mobilized the English language and sent it marching into battle in defence of freedom. Mr. Speaker, he did a great deal more. He instilled in others something of his own indomitable spirit and bulldog tenacity. That was not only Britain's finest hour, but no matter how much we may disagree

with him on other matters, that was Churchill's finest hour. No one can take it from him.
He will go down in history as a great war leader who rallied Britain and the commonwealth in their darkest hour to resist nazi aggression and restore peace to a war torn world.
In a very real sense we cannot honour this great man; his deeds have brought him honour far beyond our power to augment by words we may utter. He has won for himself a place among the great figures of history. We can here today, and we do, pay tribute to the great service he has rendered to Britain and the commonwealth, the great contribution he has made to the defence of freedom, and to what he has done for the enhancement of parliamentary institutions.
The members of the New Democratic party join, as I am sure all members of this house and all Canadians do, in expressing to Sir Winston Churchill our deepseated gratitude for a lifetime of devoted service. We express to Sir Winston and Lady Churchill the hope that they may have much health and happiness in the years that lie ahead.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON RETIREMENT FROM BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking today in place of our leader, the hon. member for Red Deer, who unfortunately is not able to be present. We in the Social Credit party wish to associate ourselves with those who today are paying tribute to one of the greatest statesmen of all time, Sir Winston Churchill, on the occasion of his retirement from active political life.
I do not intend to repeat what has been said by those who have preceded me, but I would say that the service of this great statesman to his own country and to the free world has never been equalled in the annals of history, nor is it likely to be eclipsed in any future period of time. The memory of those challenges with which he inspired courage, fortitude and the will and determination to triumph over the forces of aggression still thrills the hearts of free men everywhere. His service in various capacities, both in and outside the House of Commons, in times of peace has been an inspiration to all those who strive to fulfil the responsibilities of true and useful citizenship. I wish to read a very brief quotation from an editorial which appeared in the Calgary Albertan:
The one quality which separates great men from failures could be defined as "bounce". In the 30's Churchill was utterly defeated, ridiculed, and cast out of politics. He for a time retired to his home, took out a card as a union member, and laid bricks. Finally his moment of justification

May I say that greatness has always been his constant companion. On this occasion we extend our best wishes on his retirement from active political life, and trust that his remaining years will be brightened by the satisfaction of having served with such distinction the cause of peace and justice.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON RETIREMENT FROM BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I wish to join with the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, other party leaders and all members of the house, I am sure, to pay tribute to that great statesman, Sir Winston Churchill.
This man was prominent in many spheres and he distinguished himself in several fields, while devoting his life to the defence of two great principles he cherished: the British Empire and above all, democracy.
I think that Sir Winston had only one shortcoming, the same as the Leader of the Opposition, in this house, in that he was a Conservative all through his life.
This man was proud of his origin, of his country, of his country's institutions and he fought with courage, often against great odds, to heighten the prestige of Great Britain throughout the world.
And when, in 1939, hell broke loose in Europe, it was Sir Winston Churchill who picked up the torch of freedom and democracy to lead the whole western world into battle against Hitler's domination.
He aroused one and all to greater determination and effort until, after countless sacrifices, freedom and democracy stood triumphant.
Mr. Speaker, as any other man in public life Sir Winston Churchill may have made mistakes, taken questionable stands, but there can be no doubt in my mind that he is retiring today with a heavy balance on the credit side. He remains the symbol of the statesman standing ever upright and on guard. We of the Ralliement Creditiste are happy to associate ourselves with the tribute paid by the previous speakers and to support the motion just brought forward.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION IN CASE OF INJURY OR DEATH
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION IN CASE OF INJURY OR DEATH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since it is the duty of all citizens to assist the law enforcing authorities to maintain order, those persons who are injured in the discharge of this duty are entitled to remuneration, as are the dependants of those who are killed. This bill affirms the principle that the government has a duty to award compensation to those injured, or to the dependants of those killed, in attempting to put down crime; and it provides the procedure whereby applicants may petition the government for grace and favour compensation.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, on July 28 the hon. member for Lisgar asked me some questions about oats quotas. I can advise the house that the wheat board has advised that the quota for oats will not be raised during the remaining two days of the current crop year. The Canadian Wheat Board Act provides that only grain delivered during a crop year may be accepted into the pool account for that year. I might, however, add this. Mr. Chairman, I am
pleased to participate this afternoon in the perusal of the interim supply estimates, although I feel my inadequacy to do so. I notice that the subject estimates amount at the present time to almost $700 million, so we must agree that it is the duty of all members of parliament, above all the government itself and the Queen's loyal opposition, to remain here and deal with these vital matters pertaining to the economy of our country; and when that is done and other matters have been looked after, possibly we will deserve a short interval of leisure.
It is also a pleasure to speak this afternoon on another matter of which I have given hon. members notice through the mail. If
Interim Supply
hon. members would bear with me for a minute I should like to invite them to the Lennox and Addington-Napanee centennial, which will begin on Friday of this week and run through to August 8. We are proud that His Honour Mr. Speaker, who so ably presides over this chamber, will be our honoured guest. The county town of Napanee, which is the place of his birth, and the county of Lennox and Addington will welcome him. We are proud of him and hope his visit will be an occasion for the renewing of old acquaintances, and giving him the honour he so richly deserves.
The first day, Friday July 31, is the day of the queen's coronation ball. Saturday, August 1 is homecoming day. Sunday, August
2,	will be dedication day. Monday, August
3,	will be civic day; Tuesday, old fashioned day, followed by youth day, ladies day, agriculture and industry day, terminating with the day on which the county and town look to the future, Saturday, August 8. All hon. members are cordially invited to come down and help us celebrate our 100th anniversary. May I thank you, Mr. Chairman, and other hon. members for bearing with me in regard to this announcement.
On coming to the subject of forestry, water resources and rural development, may I say that the forest industry was well described and its activities ably portrayed yesterday by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, who was the first minister of that department and whom I congratulate in that regard. He has well laid out the position which the forest industry occupies today in our country.
I have before me, Mr. Chairman, one of our government of Canada pencils. On it appear the words "Misuse is abuse". That is a very good truism. Misuse is abuse, and this government has abused the forest industry by the misuse of the government's powers of taxation. One of the great errors committed by the government lies in the fact that it is slowly but surely crippling the forest industry, the lumbering industry and the pulp and paper industry. Our forest products industry, one of the original activities of our country, is even older than agriculture because of the necessity for first clearing land of timber before the first crops could be grown. Down through the years this industry has played a mighty part in the development of Canada. Our timber, both softwood and hardwood, has been the best in the world and has always commanded a ready sale at premium prices in the markets of the world. You can see, Mr. Chairman,

Interim Supply
how vital the continued prosperity of that industry is to every person in this country, even those who are not active in it. It, along with the great pulp and paper industry, its forest partner, has been the largest contributor toward balancing our international trade.
This government, under the system of taxation it is practising, is imposing an unjust tax on the machinery of production for this industry, as well as an 11 per cent tax on the products of the industry. This is grossly unfair, Mr. Chairman, not only to the industry itself but to the men who have worked in it and who would like to continue working in it. It is unfair also to the people who have invested their capital in the lumber industry. I believe I know whereof I speak, because I have spent 20 years in the various facets of this industry.
The taxes imposed by this government are unfair to the provincial governments of the country which are operating their respective forestry departments according to economic laws. These provincial governments are protecting public stands of timber from fire. They are practising the arts of conservation, reforestation and silviculture in all their phases. These provincial governments depend upon the controlled sale of stumpage and timber licences by public tender. If this government in Ottawa is going to continue to impose this current load of taxation on the forest industry, then those in that industry are going to cease to bid on standing timber. They are going to cease to be interested in the production of lumber, timber and other forest products.
If this situation occurs, more people will be out of work. It will sharply reduce the revenues of the provinces as well and, as is being demonstrated right now, it will markedly increase the cost of housing to the general public. This is especially burdensome to those young men and women who are starting out in life to raise a family, and who require decent accommodation in which to do so.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is another great economic field that this tax on building materials and lumber affects adversely, and that is the real estate business. I am not referring to the few people or companies who take part in the real estate business across our country. Nearly all our people are owners of some form of real estate. Under our municipal system real estate is a security for all obligations. In other words, taxable real estate is the security for raising the money a municipality needs. This undue, unjust and heavy taxation of one of the most important 
components of a house does not encourage the real estate or building industry.
At the present time the building industry is the leading factor in the production of our national wealth, and is a very great contributor to municipal revenues. I leave you with this question, Mr. Chairman. Is this government, by these measures, going to injure both the provincial and municipal economies of this country? By their misuse of the powers of taxation, which I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, are they going to dry up the springs of economic incentives upon which Canada could always rely in the past for her national development? I leave you with that question, Mr. Chairman.
I should like now to deal with water resources. The people of my county have always followed water conservation practices. The reason for the settlement of these communities along the rivers of our province lay in water power. In fact, the first industry in the town of Napanee, the ancient site of which is marked by a historic plaque, was a mill erected by the British government to keep the loyalist settlement from starving to death in 1788. I, Mr. Chairman, have had some experience in conservation, having helped to build the second Depot lake dam, which is 30 miles up river from the town of Napanee. This dam was completed in 1958 and the federal government of the day was a partner with the provincial government in the completion of that project.
With regard to the need for water resources, Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote from a clipping from the Family Herald of July 16, 1964. The headline reads "Needed, Men Who Know."
Sixty years ago President Theodore Roosevelt was preparing to call a world conference on conservation. Among things he wanted it to do were these:
1.	Prepare a general plan for an inventory of the world's resources.
2.	Recommend ways of preventing waste, and of replenishing and developing resources.
3.	Recommend that the countries of the world co-operate to safeguard and improve the basic means of their support.
4.	Draw attention to the lessons of the past regarding the wise use of resources.
I will not read all the article, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to quote this part about Canada:
It would be unfair to leave the impression that Canada has been a vacuum over these years. We have done considerable good work under prairie farm rehabilitation administration, maritime marshland reclamation association and numerous provincial conservation plans.

I note, Mr. Chairman, that the plans mentioned originated during the regime of the former government as part of their sound policy for the conservation of our water resources. I note also that there is a reference to the need for the conservation and use of our continental waters. The North American water and power alliance is prominently mentioned as the instrument for harnessing these waters for irrigation purposes across parts of our Canadian prairies. Of course the scheme includes a large amount of United States territory. In so far as acre feet are concerned, by U.S. estimates, Canada compares with the United States on the basis of approximately 10,000 to 40,000, in proposed water benefit. The United States claims about four times the water supply that can be utilized by this North American water and power alliance.
This is a vast plan that would supply the scarce parts of the two countries in so far as water is concerned. But the ratio of benefit should not be in that preponderance, for most of the water rises in Canada.
I see now the wisdom exercised by my colleague from Rosetown-Biggar, who some time ago opposed the complete utilization of Rocky mountain water under the Columbia river treaty. I can see now the wisdom of retaining some of those waters for use in the dry areas of our central plains.
Also along the line of forest conservation I should like to point out the great merit in conservation of our timber and in particular the great need for combating Dutch elm disease which is so rampant and so damaging to the elm trees of our country. In my research with regard to this matter I found that on December 10, 1962 the following question was asked by the hon. member for Cumberland, as found on page 2476 of Hansard:
1.	Has the Department of Forestry undertaken a study of the prevalence of Dutch elm disease in Canada and, if so, what is the result of such study?
2.	What is the federal government doing to eradicate Dutch elm disease?
His question was answered by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, then minister of the department, as follows:
1. The Department of Forestry has undertaken a comprehensive program of surveys and research on the Dutch elm disease and definite procedures are recommended to reduce the destructiveness of this serious disease.
It has been demonstrated that control measures involving the removal of diseased and dead trees and spraying of healthy trees with insecticides can keep losses to tolerable levels. Where these measures are not implemented, however, the disease
Interim. Supply
is expected to continue to kill elms for many years in areas where it now occurs, namely, western New Brunswick and southern Quebec and Ontario, and to spread to other areas-
It is spreading, Mr. Chairman.
-but it is unlikely that it will eliminate elms from our landscape.
Intensive research is in progress to determine how the disease develops in infected trees and on chemotherapy to find improved measures of control. Co-operative studies with Department of Agriculture scientists have resulted in the development of elms apparently resistant to the disease. These trees are presently being critically tested to determine the degree of resistance.
2. It is unlikely that the Dutch elm disease can be completely eradicated. The disease is now well established over extensive areas of Canada and the United States and under these conditions it is impossible to remove all sources of infection. The present program in many cities and park regions is one of sanitation which calls for early detection and removal of infected trees. In cities where these programs have been rigidly applied losses have been reduced to tolerable levels.
Fredericton, New Brunswick, is given as an example. Hon. members will recall that Fredericton is a beautiful city whose streets are lined with stately elms.
The federal government is assisting in control programs by providing technical assistance and guidance in methods and procedures of disease control. Extensive continuing surveys are carried out to define the limits and seriousness of the disease and to provide other information essential for timely control operations.
I ask the present government what they are doing to continue the fight to protect and preserve the elm, one of our most stately trees and of great value to the economy of the country. A good example was set by the former administration, and the people of Canada expect the present government to continue to wage war against Dutch elm disease wherever it appears in our country.
Much has been said in the past about low water, and I should like to draw attention to some of the problems in my riding. Last fall the level of lake Ontario was down in our area by approximately 40 inches or almost four feet. It has risen some this summer, but the level is still far below normal. I claim that dredging is the only answer to low water in our harbours. We are in a low water cycle at the present time, and if the water level is going to remain low for a long time dredging is the only answer in order that we may make full use of the navigation facilities in our harbours, large and small. The government should alleviate this situation by providing more money for dredging, as we are in a low water cycle and the level is not apt to rise appreciably for at least two or three years.

Interim Supply
Picton harbour in my constituency badly needs dredging. I remind hon. members that the port of Picton is the second ranking port in Ontario in tonnage because of the large shipments of iron ore and cement. I ask the government to look into the dredging of this old, useful and valuable harbour immediately because it is the key point of water shipment in our constituency and the main harbour of the county of Prince Edward.
I have one more matter to raise concerning rural development. According to the response by speakers on the government benches yesterday, it seems to be taboo to mention ARDA here, but I wish to protest the sad neglect of the government to implement the provisions of the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. It seems to me that activity in this regard has reached a very low ebb. No action is being taken by the government.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could raise a point of order at this time. The objection taken yesterday to the discussion of ARDA matters was that these items had already been dealt with by the committee of supply and a decision taken on them. That was the objection taken. If the hon. member will check the record I think he will find that on or about July 10 these items were approved by the committee of supply and a decision taken on them. There is no objection to the other part of his remarks relating to the administration of the Department of Forestry.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to venture an observation in connection with the point raised by the President of the Privy Council. I submit it to you for your consideration, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member who has the floor is speaking about the minister and his activities. Part of the activities of the minister is the administration of the Department of Forestry. I submit that as long as the hon. member is speaking of the activities by the minister he is perfectly in order, even though part of those activities were dealt with in a previous vote.

I am afraid the former minister did not get my remarks. I made it clear I had not taken objection to discussion of the ministry of forestry. I only had reason to take objection when the hon. member started to discuss the ARDA program in a particular, detailed way. It was at that point I rose.
As to the other point raised by the former minister, he will of course realize it is not usual to discuss the details of the estimates on interim supply. On a supply motion it is usual to discuss general grievances. What is asked for here is not the voting of a particular item, but permission to the government to have so much of the year's appropriations spent for a certain limited period of time.
As a protection to hon. members it is usual to give an undertaking at the start of interim supply proceedings, protecting the rights of hon. members to discuss the detail of the estimates which have not heretofore been considered.

I think the minister will agree it is not all the fault of the opposition for the confusion facing us. The government has so many ministers confused with one thing or another that it is pretty hard to decide what is the subject matter before the committee.

It is in an interim supply bill that the traditional permission is given to the government to carry on until the estimates can be brought before parliament and voted. It is quite clear when one studies the record of business this year that the estimates could not be brought before the house on the supply days because the opposition has taken the time on interim supply that should have been spent on main estimates. The opposition cannot have it both ways. They cannot prevent the estimates coming before the house by discussing interim supply, taking up days and days of time, and then claim the time allotted to supply by the government has not been used to discuss main estimates. In past years, except where there was some grievance against the government for a particular failure, to deliver a budget or something of that sort, interim supply has usually taken about 15 minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To my mind the remarks of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox to this point have been perfectly relevant, and I am quite satisfied he can continue.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. With due respect to the minister on the front bench opposite who has just interrupted, I estimate that he has been taking up the time of the committee for the last five minutes on nothing but partisan observations. It is our duty to point out the shortcomings of the government. If we do not do that then we are not doing our duty to our constituents nor to the country as a whole.

The government has announced a tew instances of activity under ARDA, and I give the ministry credit for establishing a community pasture in Algoma West at Dunns valley, only about three or four miles from where I was born. I was pleased to see some activity there, although we do not seem to be able to obtain any similar action in my constituency; but these few narrow activities are not conducive to the original, broad, permanent benefits envisaged by the act. For example, the concept of rural development has been totally forgotten. The over-all broad returns, socially and economically, that should be the accrued result of ARDA, are not being obtained by the government.
Yesterday evening hon. members paid a visit to the Laurentian hills, to Kingsmere, and we all wish to thank Mr. Speaker for his hospitality. Driving through the Gatineau park I noted the great results achieved by the national capital commission, and to that commission and its members a lot of credit should be given. Something is shown in Gatineau park of the way ARDA should function. There is the road development, to get into and out of it. The lakes and streams are in a high state of development and protection. Grazing lands are maintained for whatever use may be made of them. Then there is the recreational angle, all showing what ARDA could achieve if it were properly administered.
I have endeavoured to point out a few things as I see them and I hope that in doing so I shall have accomplished something in getting the government back on the track to administer these matters for the benefit of the country as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, since yesterday I have wanted to draw the attention of the house, as I now have the opportunity to do, to some protests I received with regard to the Department of National Revenue.
At midday today, I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) whether the county of Villeneuve had been singled out for special treatment or if orders for special inspection had been given. The minister stated that everything was taking place exactly as in other ridings.
Mr. Chairman, I have here a large file of letters from people who made certain claims at their district taxation office with regard to charitable donations. Some federal employees decided to cut down those claims.
For instance, someone claimed on the basis of attached receipts-as it should be pointed
Interim Supply
out-an amount of $300 for charitable donations. But the federal employees decided that $100 was enough. Now, everybody can claim $100 in Canada; that is the law. We certainly do not need a taxation office employee to cut down the claims of Canadian taxpayers.
I have here the case of Miss Marie-Ange Demers, from Fabre in the county of Pontiac-Temiscamingue. Instead of making her payment to the Department of National Revenue, she sends me an envelope addressed in this way:
Taxation Data Centre-Centre des donnees fis-eales-Box 475, Ottawa 2, Ontario.
A money order for $22.05 was enclosed to remit what the Department of National Revenue had claimed.
On July 21 last, that is, nine days ago, the Department of National Revenue sent her the following letter:
The amount owed is overdue. This is the last notice of payment in your case. If we do not hear from you within two weeks, legal proceedings will be instituted without further notice.
That is the way they write to a taxpayer.
The taxpayer in this case answered the Department of National Revenue quite rightly:
Sir,
X am sending you an amount of $22.05, mind you. I do not owe this amount, but my pride is worth more than that to me. What I paid on behalf of my niece exceeded $800, and, of course, I could hardly keep her with me to do her classical course, she was at school at the convent-
Miss Demers paid for her, but the taxation division does not take this into account.
Nevertheless, your conduct proves to many that you are unfair, and we shall remember this in due course.
This was written by a Canadian lady taxpayer.
Had I brought the matter before a court, I would not have been worried at all, but I am not as heartless as you are.
She is right on this point.
You are not worth our taking legal action, with such consciences as you have. I shall not allow myself to be brought before the court for so little, but what you owe me, your damned soul will not take it in eternal bliss, if you believe in the hereafter.
Mr. Chairman, this was a letter from a Canadian lady taxpayer.
On several occasions, for five or six months, we have drawn the attention of the Department of National Revenue on the fact that Canadian taxpayers are abused.

Interim Supply
I have here a letter from the deputy minister:
Following my letter dated July 6, I wish to acknowledge receipt of your subsequent letter dated July 10, concerning Miss Marie-Ange Demers, of Fabre, Temiscamingue county, province of Quebec. Miss Demers' claims for exemption concerning maintenance of her niece was carefully studied. Although an unmarried person who kept a household and has really maintained an entirely dependant person, a relative by blood, marriage, or adoption, may get an exemption of $1,000, it would seem-

I go back to my riding and I enjoy meeting my constituents again. What is important is that members of parliament should be able to spend more time in their ridings with their constituents. This government, through its bad management of the affairs of this house, has not given us an opportunity to get back to our ridings and find out what the problems are at the grass roots. We live here almost in a separate world, when we sit in this house for such a long time. I wish to pass on to the minister the suggestion that in conjunction with this forest

research laboratory there should be a forestry museum. I am sure the two members from British Columbia whom I see on the other side of the chamber will support such a project. I do not think the cost would be significant but I am sure that leadership on the part of the government is required before such a museum could be established. The provincial government will, I am sure, cooperate-I have had an indication to that effect-and certainly the forest industry of British Columbia will co-operate and contribute toward the establishment of such a forestry museum.
This will not only serve as a record of the history of forestry but will provide a tourist attraction and serve certain educational and research purposes.
The next, and main, point I want to make, Mr. Chairman, concerns the question of research in forestry. Forestry is one of the most important industries of Canada. This is signified by the fact that in 1962 the export of forest products amounted to $1.7 billion out of a total of a little over $6 billion. In British Columbia, for instance, in 1963 the net value of the forest products was $850 million. Let us refer to the main estimates for the current year, 1964-65. What do we see there? I suggest that the main point upon which the Department of Forestry should concentrate in so far as this research is concerned is the forest fire protection service. This year the federal government is providing some $8 million, for the whole of Canada, toward not only fire protection but reforestation-only $8 million for this important industry.
Representations have been made to me by the forest industry of British Columbia in this regard. The federal government needs to give leadership to the development, organization and control of a forest fire protection service adequate for the needs of Canada. I break down my point in this regard into two or three categories. The first matter to be considered is what the force requirements should be for such a research program. The house resumed from Thursday, July 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-27, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada-Mr. Brown-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Number of directors.

Mr. Chairman, I believe this is the fourth time that this bill has been before the house. It is, on the face of it, a simple bill. It increases the number of directors, or gives the company authority to increase the number of directors, from 15 to 20. The company has had authority for some years to have 20 directors. In the year 1927 it brought its directorate up to 15 in number, but since then the company has felt that it is in its own interests to have a greater range of representation on the board from different parts of the country, consisting of men with experience. The debate so far has been protracted and has taken a form not anticipated at the beginning, in spite of a rather lengthy debate before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, which gave detailed consideration to the matters at issue on July 27.
I want to touch on three basic points which have been made in this debate. The last time this committee considered the matter, on July 23, the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm put on the record the names and biographies of all of the directors of the company. His purpose in doing so, I inferred from reading the record, was to establish two things. First of all he cited the business associations of the directors, and somehow appeared to be criticizing the company for leaning too heavily on business experience, suggesting that this was perhaps a conspiracy of some kind. It is rather novel to criticize a private company for having men of business experience of this standard. Perhaps they are too competent, or something; I am not quite sure what was the inference to be drawn.
The second criticism of the hon. gentleman was that he felt there was inadequate representation on the board of directors of persons whose mother tongue was French. The company intends to do what it can

Private Bills
to deal with this second criticism. The president of the company is a man whose mother tongue is French, Mr. Marcel Vincent. I think the company has tried carefully and assiduously to follow a satisfactory program of public relations and do what is fair and proper in this matter.
I am very much concerned at the form of the debate, which has taken a demagogic turn. Some of the things which have been said simply are not true. I remember at one point I rose in protest at what I considered to be unfair and improper treatment of the company, and I was surprised by some interjections from some hon. members opposite, including the hon. member for Victoria, (Ont.), who asked whether or not I had shares in the company. I should like to make my motives for objecting quite clear at this point; they do not spring from any private ownership of shares or interest in the company.
I have another reason for objecting, one of which I am not ashamed, and that is that in my riding there is a fairly substantial operation conducted by the Northern Electric Company, a subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company. The relationship between Northern Electric and Bell has been debated before the committee. There are those who would move quickly in this matter and adopt the very simple solution of nationalization. I am not one who believes that there are not situations where public operations are not very useful or efficient, and I do not agree with my colleague from Jacques Cartier-Lasalle in some of his denunciations of crown corporations and his comment that they are always losing money. They are not. Many of them are proper operations of which we have every reason to be proud.
Those who have a simple answer to the problem of communications, namely the nationalization of industry, I think are deluding themselves. In my own riding I have visited the installation of the research and development branch of Northern Electric. They run an export business, including exports to the United States, amounting to something like $8 million a year. They are a company which a couple of months ago had an export order for an item of equipment to the United States of America amounting to $400,000. They make video installations and communications systems which they sell to all parts of the United States. The major market which they are developing is one which leans towards the relatively low volume, long distance type of problem, which is peculiarly a Canadian problem. The research which is developed and oriented in this direction makes it a very important arm of participation in certain types of export business. Its export business is its bread and butter and provides jobs to many of the people I represent.
I have a serious doubt in my mind whether the abrupt nationalization of this organization would be at all beneficial. There is a pattern sharing arrangement involved in which 1 per cent of gross revenue is contributed and the benefits of broad research are shared. I think that disruption of such an operation would do a great deal of damage, and a great deal of the very intensive concentration upon exports in a highly competitive field might be jeopardized. I appreciate there are certain members on the other side of the house, for whom I have great respect, who think they have found a simple, routine, monopolistic formula, that of nationalization, which seems to be somewhat doctrinaire. However, the province from which most of the members of that group come has had recent cause to discover the benefits of private enterprise.
The Bell Telephone Company is contributing to a field of research which is part of an over-all agreement on specialization and research and is doing a good job and employing many people in my riding. It pays good wages, conducts a good operation and has good relations with its employees. As far as I am concerned I find a great deal to commend in this.
Many other things, Mr. Chairman, have been said loosely. For example the charge is made that the rates are high. There is a board of transport commissioners in Canada. There is an Ontario and Quebec schedule, a schedule of the national system of eight major participating telephone companies, and the board of transport commissioners has a responsibility to look at those rates. Rates even with the United States are regulated by the federal communications commission and the board of transport commissioners. I submit it is not the function of this committee at this time and place to review the operations of the board of transport commissioners. It may be that we need to do something about them. Perhaps the job is not done as effectively as it might be, and if that is the case there is another item of business for the house to consider.
There are one or two fundamental matters in connection with the scale of charges. The same issue is raised in communications as in many other operations of public utilities. This

Private Bills
company paid $63 million by way of income tax last year. According to the 1963 annual report, total taxes were something of the order of $84 million. Income tax on each main telephone in a private home amounted to $22.50; that is without considering extensions. It is superficially easy to say that if a company is nationalized this type of income tax ceases to be a charge on the company, that the consumer gets more of a break, and what a grand thing it is.
We have to face the broader problem of the incidence of taxation. How is this parliament going to raise the money to conduct its operations? If you do not get the money here, you will have to get it somewhere else. If taxes are not collected in this way, they will be levied in another way. The problem is the broader problem of the incidence of taxation. The question of how as a matter of policy to deal with the effect of the incidence in regard to the taxation of a public utility of this nature is a very broad problem; it is not easily or superficially solved.
It is easy to be demagogic, Mr. Chairman. It is easy to denounce this company. It is easy to denounce as inhumane treatment its policy of not allowing its subscribers to run up a bill. It is easy to find instances of alleged bureaucratic treatment of its subscribers which are not justified by standards of humanity, as mentioned by one hon. member opposite. This company, Mr. Chairman, in its operations has had a record in this country of progressive and vigorous investment in the extension of its services. Telephone services in Canada are being extended at a much greater rate than the rate of increase in the population. In the last five years over a billion dollars has been expended by the Bell Telephone Company itself in the extension of its facilities. Whatever are its faults, it represents the type of industry, the type of development, which I feel has an honourable place in most Canadian communities.
This company comes to this chamber to ask permission to add five more members to its board of directors. I feel that such a measure should be passed by the house. I should like to make one other observation. I do not believe that hon. members opposite, and I am looking at the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, are doing a great service by demagogically attacking this company. If they wish to continue that attack, if they wish to nationalize the company within the province of Quebec, it is their privilege to do so. They are perfectly

within their rights to introduce the necessary legislation in the provincial legislature.
I would say to this company: My riding is proud of the jobs you have created; bring your head office to Ottawa and it will be very welcome. You will not be subjected to the same harassment as you are in the place in which you have chosen to locate. Come to this community and bring those jobs, bring the establishment here and, I can assure you, you will get a welcome. You will receive treatment which will be in accordance with those traditions of fair play which I feel are best for Canadian development.

Mr. Chairman, I respect the views just expressed by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) even if I do not agree with them unreservedly.
The Bell Telephone Company of Canada has been a great success and is giving very good service to the Canadian people. That is a fact. But what is helping this company to a great extent is that, in the city of Montreal, for instance, there is no competition whatsoever. Now, when a company has no competitors, it is much easier to operate and make profits.
Still better, Mr. Chairman, when the federal government needs the services of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, when crown corporations like the C.B.C. and the telecommunication board or the Department of National Defence want it for the D.E.W. or Pine Tree lines, no public tender is asked, and the government and the crown corporations have to accept the price set by the Bell Telephone Company.
Another matter I should like to point out to the hon. member for Carleton is that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is the owner of the Northern Electric Company. Approximately 65 per cent of all material it buys, whether it be cables, wires or appliances, are purchased from its subsidiary, the Northern Electric Company, and not by means of public tender. When the Bell Telephone Company of Canada appears before the board of transport commissioners to ask permission to increase its rates, its representatives say to the commissioners: "Well, this year, this appliance is costing us 50 cents more than last year." However, the company did not ask for public tenders. The president of a large Canadian company in the province of Ontario came to see me recently to call my attention to this anomaly.
