Why not leave the matter to the choice of the French Canadian employees, since both languages are official in the province of Quebec? Why then compel the French-Canadian employees to write their reports in English?
Why is it that the Bell Telephone Company of Canada refuses promotions to some French Canadians, several of whom are qualified and experienced? Those employees are presently at the bottom of the scale while they deserve some promotions?
It is a fine thing that Mr. Marcel Vincent was named president and director of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, but why is discrimination to a certain extent practised against French Canadians and why does the company refuse to give them important positions in its offices?
Mr. Chairman, those were the comments I wanted to make.
I believe it would be in the public interest for the government to set up a joint Senate and Commons committee to revise the charter of the Bell Telephone Company, in order to prevent the nationalization of the said company, something about which some hon. members do not want to hear.
No Canadian company, Mr. Chairman, has so little competition in its field of activity as this one. As I said a while ago, in the city of Montreal, it controls everything, it has no competition.
But if the Bell Telephone Company of Canada wants to win the public's sympathy and the government wants to prevent its nationalization, a joint Senate and Commons committee must be set up as soon as possible, to revise the charter of the company and adapt it to circumstances. I am convinced that the company would not feel any worse for it and that the Canadian people would be happier, as well as the other companies.

Mr. Chairman, I would imagine that in the course of a normal session many similar bills are brought before the house for our approval. Since this bill is a very simple one it would be approved in a relatively short time under normal circumstances. However that is not exactly the case with this bill, which is being discussed for the fourth time because it involves the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, a company which in the eyes of some members over the last few sessions is guilty of something.
I should like to preface my remarks by saying that I have sat here rather innocently with no particular axe to grind listening to the debate in the last three weeks. I am not a shareholder of the Bell Telephone Company nor do I ever intend to be. But I did take the trouble to read the debate in Hansard to find out precisely why the Bell Telephone Company in Canada is being singled out for treatment of this type and for the retardation of what seems on the surface to be a very normal request.
I am sure that all hon. members of the house are aware of the fact that the Bell Telephone Company is asking for an increase in the

Private Bills
number of directors from 15 to 20. Bills of this type appear before us quite often as companies try to reorganize their internal structures to meet the ever increasing demands of business, and I think the reasons behind the request for the increase were very well explained by the Bell spokesmen when the bill was considered by a committee. But I did manage to summarize as briefly as I could the reasons why the Bell Telephone Company has been singled out for particular scrutiny, particularly by my good friend, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. He has repeated quite often that the Bell Telephone Company is guilty of being a big company and of making big profits.
He is a little man.

He has said it is guilty of being monopolistic, and guilty of giving inadequate opportunities for promotion to French Canadians. He repeated the last charge a few moments ago. It was not my intention to deal with it first, but in view of the fact that he has repeated it I should like to deal with it now.
Whenever on rare occasions I have spoken in this house, I have never hesitated to express my admiration, indeed my affection, for the people of French Canada. This is natural since, as I have said on many occasions, I come from that province and in certain milieus I am considered more French than English. But I hate the type of generalization engaged in by speaker after speaker from the province of Quebec when they get up and say this company or that company is denying French Canadians their rights, and then do not document their charges. This is very unfair not only to the company concerned but, what is more dangerous, it is very unfair to French Canadians, because it is creating an illusion among people who read the daily papers or who read Hansard and follow the proceedings of the house that everyone in French Canada is placing the blame for his normal failures-we all have them, English or French-strictly at the feet of big companies, big enterprises, when I happen to know this is not the fact. It might possibly be the fact in a particular case, but when the hon. member gets up and says that the Bell Telephone Company-I tried to take note of his words-denies promotion to people within the company simply because they are French Canadians, I challenge the hon. member to prove it.

Ask the employees of the company.
tMr. Mackasey.]

I would point out to the hon. member who has just interrupted me that this is one private company in Canada which is certainly not guilty of what he has suggested on many occasions in the house, not giving French Canadians the opportunity to lead and direct big business. The gentleman who is the president of the Bell Telephone Company happens to be a French Canadian, but instead of expressing pride in his accomplishments the hon. member indirectly accuses him of discrimination against his own people in the company he leads. What kind of charge is that to make against such a man?
One question, Mr. Chairman.
When I am finished.
One short question.
Order.

I notice you are fidgeting, Mr. Chairman, and no doubt about to remind me that maybe I am off the subject. Perhaps I am, but it is only in retaliation to remarks that have been made by previous speakers. In case the hon. member thinks that I alone hold these views and having in mind that the hon. member, who looks after his interests so very well in his riding, comes from a farming area, I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Rural Co-Operator of July 21 last, a newspaper which is published by the Ontario federation of agriculture. They have this to say in part:
We never thought the day would come when we would feel it necessary to defend a large private enterprise corporation. But then, we never thought the day would come when an allegedly Conservative member of parliament would demand the nationalization of that same corporation.
I am too fair a member, Mr. Chairman, to assume that because one member expresses these views he represents the views of his party. I have full respect for the Conservative party. Indeed I have full respect for the party which openly preaches socialism and nationalization. This newspaper obviously has great respect for the Conservative party because in the editorial the word "allegedly" is used in reference to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. The editorial is fairly lengthy and I will not read further from it. It makes the same accusation I have made, that when the hon. member constantly speaks about the plight of French Canada he consciously and intentionally or unintentionally fails to document his case.
If I thought that discrimination was being practised against Canadians because they

were French or English, I would be the first member of the house to stand up, whether I was in order or out of order, and express my opinion.
One question, Mr. Chairman.

I feel that such spokesmen as the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm would be able to do more for the wonderful people of the province of Quebec by being factual and intelligent about these matters.
May I address a short question to the hon. member?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Verdun has the floor. I should like to remind him that he should confine his remarks to the principle of the bill before us. As long as he speaks about members of the company who are directors I suppose he is within the ambit of the bill, but he should try to keep that in mind.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.
The hon. member referred to an editorial concerning the Bell Telephone Company. I want to say that I spoke in my own name, according to my own conscience, as if there was no problem in Canada at the present time, and I ask a question-
Order.
Why do we have a royal commission on bilingualism if we do not face a problem?

This is not a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. I would be very happy at any time to discuss and debate the plight of French Canadians and the question of bilingualism and biculturalism with the hon. member, in public, because I fully believe in the two official languages of this country and I have been consistent in my support of that position. But I repeat what I have already said twice, that constant attacks of the type engaged in by the hon. member and of the type which members in the far corner made in the debate last week do no credit to the people of Quebec and are very unfair to French Canadians. I would say that people like Elliott Trudeau are people who represent Quebec properly and adequately, and you can take a lesson from them.
Private Bills
One of the other accusations made by the hon. member concerns the exorbitant profit Bell Telephone Company makes. What is this profit? It is $68 million, a very impressive sum of money. Like a big financier, which I am not, I may be out a million or two, but what happens to this $68 million? It is redistributed to the people of Canada in the form of dividends, not people outside the country, because over 93 per cent of the shareholders of the Bell company are residents of Canada.
What more do we want out of a big company in a country that prides itself on free enterprise? Many companies make profits like this and the problem is to keep those profits in this country; but we do not have that problem with the Bell company.
If anybody wants to take the trouble to look at their annual report he will find that just a little over 6 per cent is the relation between its profit and invested capital. Anybody who knows a little about private industry, about the stock market, about the indices we regard as measures of success or failure, knows 6 per cent is not adequate, and even the student of the most elementary economics or accounting knows there must be these types of benevolent monopolies in certain fields, and Bell telephone is admittedly such a monopoly-
One of the biggest.

But there are still hundreds of small companies around the country. I respect the hon. gentleman who has just interrupted me. He did not come into the House of Commons under false pretences. He came here as a socialist and he will go out of here as a socialist, and if his party is ever in power it will nationalize this company. This is not a question of deception. He presented himself to the people of his riding in precisely those terms and they chose to elect him. I respect that; but when members from the Conservative party and the Liberal party come here as champions of private enterprise and they preach something different in this chamber, then I say they are the ones who are the hypocrites, not myself or the members in the far corner. I respect the hon. gentleman's opinion and I am sure we will hear from him in a standing position very shortly.
If by some disaster Bell were converted into a crown corporation it would remedy none of the problems mentioned by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. It would be just as big as it is now. It would be making profits, but perhaps not as many because it would not be efficiently operated.

Private Bills
It would have to be monopolistic, and we must remember that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm rises almost daily in this chamber to criticize the C.B.C., the C.N.R. and other government organizations as being anti-French, and if this company were converted into a crown corporation it would still be the subject of such criticism by the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) was dishonest with me in his observations and I would ask him to quote one reference where I made such specific remarks concerning the use of both languages.
I am in favour of the use of both languages, but I am also in favour of seeing the French Canadians in the province of Quebec, owning their share of the company-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not think this is a question of privilege.
I will not be lectured by the hon. member for Verdun.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If I may-

I should take this occasion to remind the hon. member for Verdun that we are discussing a bill that refers to an increase in the number of directors.

Mr. Chairman, you did not have to change from French to English for my benefit. I am bilingual and I uphold the theory that as a Canadian I have the right to speak my language, and that a French Canadian has the right to speak his, and that as a parliamentarian it is my duty to understand him, as it is his to understand me. This is what is to be expected in this modern day and age.
In order not to be accused of speaking too long, and perhaps in the vain hope that this bill may be discussed on its merits, I express the hope that the committee may be as fair to the Bell company as it is to all other companies that come before us with this type of request. As was pointed out by a Bell spokesman in the committee, the purpose of increasing the board of directors is to give the various vice presidents of this vast enterprise an opportunity to sit on the board of directors and spend some time there in order that they may become more fully aware of the operating of such a wonderful tribute to Canadian endeavour. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

I am very interested to note that each of these five additional directors is to do a specific job, and on this basis I presume the whole matter of the Bell Telephone Company is wide open. But the reason for increasing the directorate of the company escapes me and it probably escapes everyone else, so far as the government of Canada is concerned. However, so far as Bell is concerned it probably means they are going to take over another company or two. It is quite normal when you take over a company that you make a new director and you allow him some status because of his newly acquired shares. This might allow me to spend the next 20 minutes discussing the Osgoode Telephone Company which, according to the local newspaper, has been the subject of some lengthy discussion. In fact the new director may be the President of the Privy Council of Canada.
If this is true, and knowing the fact that the hon. gentleman sat in this house when the late C. D. Howe was the dominant factor in the business world, and knowing the Liberal government, which does not believe in the nationalization process, which is a champion of free enterprise, which believes that $68 million derived from a public utility is a normal, reasonable and acceptable thing, then I would imagine that the 113 crown corporations which previously existed under a Liberal government may be added to by the inclusion of the Bell Telephone Company through the devious method of taking over the Osgoode rural telephone exchange and making its principal owner a director. In this way the whole Bell Telephone Company may be nationalized. If my reasoning were that round about I would think this was a good idea and we would hope there would be a nationalization of the Bell company in the very near future.
This is not just another company. We are not being asked for just another five directors. When appointing directors to a company obviously you are designing what the policy of the company will be. When you ask to increase the number of directors of a corporation you are really saying there has to be some change in the control of that corporation.
I think this is true of the Bell Telephone Company. I do not believe the Osgoode Telephone Exchange will make much difference to them. I know they have taken over many small outfits across the country in the past and I think it is a fact that after their purchase of these small exchanges they have added or dropped a director for this purpose.

But, in the main, they have brought good service and we are not condemning the company in this respect.
I think it is true to say that Trans-Canada Air Lines provided a very good service for the Canadian people in a field of public monopoly, even though the monopoly is not total. Of course, the Bell Telephone Company does not operate in a complete monopoly field, either. Consideration has been given by the directors to many of the problems of modernization and expansion. But what have these directors really done in terms of satisfying the needs of the Canadian people? Here is a field in which we should show some interest. I would like one of the new directors to be given responsibility for handling a problem which is becoming increasingly apparent to me and to everyone concerned. In my view, the type of automation which has been put into effect by the company has prevented the individual subscriber from dealing effectively with anyone in authority in the company. If one of these directors is to be made responsible for liaison between the subscriber and the company, I think it constitutes a very good amendment. I do not know whether the sponsor can say that this is to be the case. I do know that according to the normal process of law anyone having a complaint against the Bell Telephone Company should have certain rights. I may say this is hypothetical in my own case because I seldom use the services of this company. I have a credit card with a company which operates in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. It operates efficiently and, I may say at once, it has a monopoly in that area, so I do not exclude it from the generality of the remarks I am making. I think they, too, might be included in a monopoly under a crown corporation if we could persuade the majority of members of parliament that this would be in the best interests of subscribers and Canadians generally and, yes, even of the shareholders. However, as I say, I have not been told whether one of these directors-he could be French, or English, or from Timbuktu if he wishes- would act as a liaison officer and give subscribers the right to have their views heard.
If a subscriber wishing to complain about a charge, or about a long distance call which had not been placed, could get in effective touch with someone in authority about it, or use some reasonable organizational method of having the grievance redressed, I would feel there might be some justification for increasing the size of the board of directors.
Private Bills
What is the position now? One can go to the board of transport commissioners. I am familiar with the case of a secretary here in the House of Commons who shared an apartment with another girl. When the other girl left, she gave to this girl who remained a sum of money which, she said, should cover the long distance calls. It subsequently turned out that the money was not enough. The company cut the telephone off and proceeded to collect from the girl who did not incur the charge in the first place and to whom the telephone was not registered. She complained to the board of transport commissioners in 1962, and the case has not yet been settled. The board said it was a very interesting case. The lawyers from the Bell Telephone Company said they would have to have time to consider it further. I could read the record of the whole case, but I would have the trouble of putting "the board of directors" in every few minutes so as to remain in order, and for this reason I will forgo this delightful exercise. But in view of the length of that procedure, if one of these directors would take over this particular function of the board by dealing genuinely with grievances, we might be getting some place.
As I began to explain a few minutes ago, normally if a member of the public has reason to complain against the service or charges of a public utility he is able to go to court and plead his case. He is also able to obtain a writ obliging the utility concerned to provide him with service while awaiting the result of the litigation. But the Bell Telephone Company is so autocratic and distant from its subscribers that the telephone is buzzed off and on, in accordance with an order from Montreal operated by a computer system without any reference to the situation locally. I do not deny that the system is a modern one, further advanced than that used by most of the other telephone companies in North America and, no doubt, much more modern than the equipment used by crown corporations which operate telephone systems in England and other countries abroad. Nevertheless its use has eliminated many things which we believe are our right, and one of these is the right to litigation without loss of service.
When a subscriber complains to a telephone company about being charged for a long distance call he is not saying he will not pay the charge; he is saying he did not make it, and therefore should not pay for it, or he is advancing some similar argument.

Private Bills
I do not think service should be discontinued until the case has been disposed of. At present, if a subscriber eventually proves his case all that happens is that he is charged another $5 and the service is buzzed back on.
I have been to meetings of boards of directors on several occasions and found that they knew as little about the operation of the business as I did. I can assure hon. members, of course, that they knew a great deal more about the financial aspects than I did, but they did not know anything more about the actual operations of the company. At one time, when I was negotiating with a mining company, I had the notion to buy a few shares so that I could attend directors' meetings. Someone said: You do not have to do that; you can attend those meetings anyway. Well, I attended one of those meetings and I came away knowing less about the actual operation of the company, after I had listened to all the financial gobbledygook, than when I entered. This is often the case with company directors. In this instance we have not been told why they are required.
Could the hon. member not have attended the meeting on railways, canals and telegraph lines and asked these interesting questions when the officials were present?
I am sure they do not know themselves, or in any case they would not tell you.
The hon. member could have been present and asked those questions when the officials were there, available to him. I wish he had done that.

In a very nice way I could ask the sponsor of the bill to tell me these things. Obviously he should know, or he would not come before parliament to ask that it be passed. But I do not wish to embarrass him because I am sure he has not been told these things and I am sure the officials would not tell me or anyone else about them.
There is another matter I wish to raise and it was touched upon by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. Unlike the previous speaker, I do not give a hoot why he has changed his mind. I am aware he represents a certain element of the province of Quebec which now believes that some of the things which were formerly done by private enterprise might be done as well, or better, by a public utility. I do not wish to enter upon a discussion of what the province of Quebec may, or may not do, but it seems to me the province got into the field of public

utilities when a crown corporation was set up to take over the hydro operation. Many people in the province held the view that the hydro operation was being conducted efficiently at a considerable profit. It may be that the board of directors was working most efficiently. However, there were many others in the province who believed that a crown corporation should be established to develop hydro as a public utility. An election was fought on this issue, and the majority decided that the better way of operating hydro was through the establishment of an agency of government.
So there may be a change in the thinking of the people of Quebec, which I am very happy to see. I am not going to question why the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm may have had this change of heart, but I welcome it. One hon. gentleman has said that we should document some of the things we have. I have before me a letter that went to a Liberal member, the hon. member for Welland, from the Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers. I am sure this matter involves the board of directors because it is directly concerned with the operation of the Bell Telephone Company. This letter was written for a very good reason and I think every member should know about it and learn what the union has to say about this matter. The letter reads in part:
It has recently been brought to the attention of members of our union who are employed in maintaining and operating the Welland ship canal that the present telephone system for inter-office, inter-structure communication, which is owned and operated by the St. Lawrence seaway authority is to be contracted out to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
It goes on:
We wish to protest in the strongest possible manner the contracting out of work which has always been done, and is still being done by employees of the seaway authority on the Welland ship canal.
We also wish to raise several questions which we believe to be pertinent at this time. The first is, "whether it is the policy of the government to encourage, assist and support the development of monopolies".
Of course, Mr. Chairman, I am sure the five new directors of this company believe in the free enterprise system and the nonmonopoly system which goes hand in hand with free enterprise. They do not ask for subsidies in closed corporations and one-industry monopolies but, of course, enjoy the free enterprise system which means, as I understand it, a competitive system, dog eat dog. This letter goes on:

The Bell Telephone Company enjoys an almost complete monopoly in the field of telephone communication in Ontario, and in many other places, it is in fact one of the, if not the largest monopoly in any service industry. The second is, "was Bell Telephone Company the only company invited to submit a bid, or was the proposed change put out for bids and any other company interested in the communication field invited to bid?"
It goes on to state why the seaway authority established their own system of telephone communication. This letter was sent to a Liberal member. I should be very interested to know-I should point out that I received a copy of it from the brotherhood- what his reply was to the brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order; I wonder just what this document and the reply of the hon. member for Welland has to do with an increase in the number of directors of Bell Telephone.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman; this is a very important matter, in my opinion, concerning the philosophy of the Bell Telephone Company. We are now being asked to approve an increase in the number of directors of this company, the appointment of five more directors, making the board comprise 20 directors instead of 15. I am wondering whether this new board of directors is going to change the philosophy of the company, which has resulted in the government co-operating with the Bell Telephone to eliminate the need for bids, or whether this means a change of policy. I believe I am perfectly in order in discussing this matter until we are informed whether the new additions to the board of directors will indicate a change in the desire for a service monopoly in the telephone field. I submit this is in order because of the fact that the sponsor of the bill has not really indicated what the new directors are going to present in the way of policy, and so on. I submit these points on the point of order, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member just has another minute or so to go. Perhaps he might complete his remarks at this time.

I think this is a very important field, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps the committee asked these questions. I do not happen to be a member of that committee, but I would suggest this matter be referred back to the committee for further discussion. If that is done, I will take the opportunity given me by the sponsor of this bill to ask these questions, and I am sure he will inform his principals
Private Bills
of the line of questioning and they will be prepared to answer these questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, I found myself quite intrigued by the remarks made a little earlier by the hon. member for Verdun when he took to task the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm for the interest he was showing in particular aspects of this matter. I have been looking over the terms of the bill rather closely, in the light of what the hon. member had to say. He made some considerable parade of his own strong support for free enterprise. He went so far as to recognize the right of other members to hold different opinions, but as I think of the policies that have from time to time been advocated by Liberal administrations in this country I rather wonder whether all the Liberal members of the house hold such strong views about the virtues of pure free enterprise as were expounded by the hon. member for Verdun.
It has occurred to me-and I would like to take the moment or two that remain at my disposal to throw this suggestion out for the consideration of the committee-that the proposal which we have before us offers interesting possibilities for what we might call assisting the development of the mixed economy in Canada, and might even meet the objections raised earlier by the hon. member for Carleton in respect of disturbing certain of the existing operations of this company. This bill, as has been mentioned quite a number of times, has to do with an alteration to the composition of the board of directors of this company. It is clear to me from the reading of the bill that it provides that the determination of who the additional directors are to be, as it is set out in the bill, is left entirely in the hands of the shareholders of the company. But I think it might be quite possible and appropriate for this committee to consider the idea of amending the terms of this clause so that in the course of increasing the number of directors to 20 we could provide that at least 10 of those directors might be appointed on the determination of this house or the government of Canada. In other words, I think this question of public ownership and the pros and cons of whether it is advisable in the monopoly utility situation is very germane to the terms of the bill.
I would suggest that prior to the time this bill comes before us for consideration again, members of the house who are concerned

Interim Supply
with such matters and with the pros and cons thereof might be prepared to give serious consideration to the suggestion I put forward at this point, and perhaps we could give some thought to the idea of introducing appropriate amendments to the bill which would put into effect the suggestion I have advocated.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
House again in committee of supply; interim supply. It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock this afternoon, I began to talk about a matter which, in my opinion, is very important, in particular for the rural areas of eastern Canada.
This coming August or September there will be a federal-provincial conference on rural development. I intended to take part in the debate yesterday but as I had to leave at 4.30, I postponed my intervention until today. I sincerely deplore the absence of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) but I am convinced that he will take note of the few remarks I intend to make to enable him at this federal-provincial conference on rural development to express the views of hon. members; that is why I want to let the minister who is now responsible for ARDA know about them.
In order to do this, I will quote the following paragraph from Mr. Claude Ryan's column which appeared in Le Devoir of March 6, 1964:
Planning will be done with the interested parties or a monstrous bureaucracy will ensue. We have been told that, in a certain Quebec area, young theorists, working for ARDA, lost the sympathy of the people in that area by acting towards them in a haughty and self-assertive manner. The "Ca-nayens"-
I am quoting the exact word or the word in quotation marks-
-in spite of the reputation of docility we are trying to attribute to them, do not like to be led by the nose, especially by civil servants.
You are aware, Mr. Chairman, that prior to the 1963 election, the Conservative government, who was presiding over the destinies of this country, had created a plan which is now known as ARDA. Indeed, on December 15, 1960, the then minister of agriculture put forward this measure which is bound to become, in a way, the Magna Carta of agriculture, especially as far as eastern Canada is concerned.
I should like to repeat here what I have already said several times, in this house as well as outside: The farmers will find in this

legislation, known as ARDA, a plan created in 1960, co-ordination principles and systems which will enable them to set in motion a real rural development campaign.
Everyone must take part in this campaign, that is the farmer, the parish, the area, the province as well as farm organizations.
In this connection, I have said and repeated on various occasions that when it introduced this legislation the Progressive Conservative government of the time did not intend to intrude in any way on the freedom of action of farmers and provinces. The aim of this legislation is to provide farmers with the technical and financial assistance which will enable them with their free will, their knowledge and their social and professional organizations to work for unity and the survival of farming generally. When I read that article under the heading "Bloc-notes" of Le Devoir, I remembered the warning which I gave this government during the throne speech debate in the first session following the 1963 election.
At that time I said this:
I now ask the government which presides over the destiny of Canada to remember that such a program of action calls upon all the human, natural, industrial and institutional resources of the community. The government will have to act but it must leave to the individuals, to private enterprise and to the co-operatives their own responsibilities. Furthermore it will have to help them by trusting them and refraining from submitting the resources of the community to harsh regulations that would kill our farmers' legitimate ambitions and, should changes take place too quickly, miss the objectives aimed at.
Mr. Chairman, in October 1962 the federal government entered into agreements with every Canadian province.
They were signed with the full assurance that the federal government would leave each province entirely free to choose the urgent projects. In 1963 when the Conservative party was defeated, we heard statements like that made by Mr. Davidson which was prepared for the standing committee of the Canadian farmers' federation studying rural development. What did he say on April 6, 1963? Here are his words:
As far as I know, there never existed closer federal-provincial co-operation for the application of a joint program. Federal-provincial relations about that program are good in general and that augurs well for the success of those joint programs.
And agreements were signed between the federal government and the province. There is a table which is available to all members upon request to the regional director of ARDA. As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, on December 6, 1962, the govern-
Interim Supply
ment approved and signed a convention with the province of Quebec for the making of a survey by the province at the cost of $185,000 to which the federal government was to contribute 50 per cent or $92,500. On January 1963, the federal government sent that convention to the government of the province of Quebec for signature.
We see that as far as Quebec is concerned, on January 7, an agreement was signed with the federal government, and after January, a second, a third, a fourth and a fifth and on February 27, 1963, there was an agreement on rural development.
As requested at the beginning of April 1963, an agreement was approved by the representatives of ARDA in my own riding of Nicolet-Yamaska, concerning the dredging of two creeks. That is to say, Mr. Chairman, that when our hon. friends opposite came to power a complete agreement was arrived at between the provincial and federal governments, according to the data given by the ARDA director. I should like to be permitted to mention again the words of the director:
-there never existed closer federal-provincial co-operation for the application of a joint program.
And at the end of his statement to the Canadian farmers' federation, he said:
Consequently, it is important to strengthen mutual understanding between the federal government and the provinces with respect to the objectives of the program before ARDA agreements are renegotiated in 1965 or 1966.
What happened since the institution of the famous co-operative federalism on April 22, 1963? The provinces, especially Quebec, have started complaining that the central government is trying to force its wishes upon them with respect to the administration of ARDA. That is so true that at the end of another of his statements made on February 6, 1964, just a few months ago, ARDA director Davidson stated:
I have tried to cover a lot of ground but I have refrained on purpose from dealing with the very important and most interesting problem of federal-provincial relations and the more pragmatic questions raised by co-operative federalism.
In any case, I hope I have given you a general idea of the kind of problems we are up against and I also hope that my remarks will give rise to some discussions.
I have a few excerpts here from statements which have appeared in the press. For instance, this large headline in UAction of July 6, 1964:
Ottawa will not intervene in Quebec ARDA projects.

Interim, Supply
Agreements signed between the provinces and the federal government clearly stipulated that programs put forward under ARDA would not be imposed on the provinces and that furthermore, under ARDA no plans or projects would be imposed on municipalities but that municipalities would be assisted in the development of plans and projects.
In another daily, that is he Devoir of July 6, 1964, we read the following:
Rural development: from now on Ottawa will respect Quebec-Summit conference to convene this summer.
We see such public statements only since co-operative federalism was introduced and since our Liberal friends came to power and we seriously wonder why the provinces, and more particularly the province of Quebec, have come to the point of refusing the Minister of Forestry or the federal government the right to put their noses into projects which have to be determined on its own by the province. And, we further wonder whether the federal government did not want to impose its will with regard to those ARDA projects. This is what we read in La Terre de Chez Nous, a farming publication of the Canadian farmers' union of July 22, 1964, under the title:
Parliament in action-Farming.. .from the Quebec angle.
In an item prepared by the provincial information service, we find this:
At the federal-provincial conference scheduled for August or September, which will consider this country's farming problems, and more particularly the suggested amendments to the agreements under ARDA for rural development, it is foreseen and accepted by now that Quebec will claim the privilege of determining urgent projects on its own.
And I repeat "determine urgent projects on its own". In Quebec, it is admitted that the province will demand that privilege. We know that as from October 1962 under Conservative rule, each province was free to determine any urgent or emergency project on its own, whereas today, under Liberal rule, with cooperative federalism, provinces have to tell the federal government: We are going to claim our rights and determine matters of urgency ourselves.
And it goes on. The article was based on information received from the provincial government.
Since 1961, Ottawa has forced projects upon the provinces, but there is every indication that, following Quebec's representations this attitude will change.
Last Friday, on July 24, I asked the Minister of Forestry the following question:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Forestry who is responsible for rural development.
Could the Minister of Forestry tell me whether, at the present time, the provinces, by virtue of agreements entered into in connection with ARDA, determine themselves the urgent projects for rural development or whether it is the Ottawa government which imposes those projects on the provinces?
And the Minister of Forestry answered.
Mr. Speaker, the provinces take the lead in this field.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that that answer is correct. I am convinced that, in the spirit of the legislation as passed by the house in 1961, the federal government actually had the intention of leaving that responsibility completely and entirely with the provinces. But today, we ask ourselves this question. Why must the provinces ask the federal government to respect the agreements entered into in October 1962?
Mr. Chairman, during that federal-provincial conference on rural redevelopment, the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, will study the program to be implemented as from the month of April 1965.
Such a program, for instance, might also provide for an improvement of public credit.
The federal farm credit was improved and the province of Quebec has an efficient system of loans for the farmers. But credit should be made available to some organizations so that they could do their job. In fact, it will be recalled that, in 1962, the Conservative government made an amount of $50 million available to the administrators of the ARDA program. That amount is at their disposal until 1965, in order to assist the provinces in the reorganization of their own territory. But they should also have available to them some money which would permit them to raise the standard of living in some regions.
In the statement to which I referred, it is also said:
We will also consider the matter of a comprehensive forestry redevelopment program in rural areas, not only as a land use project, but through the planting of trees and forestry improvement.
On that matter, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister responsible for the administration of ARDA.
I wonder if, in the course of the studies conducted by the federal and provincial governments in order to define the urgent projects, it would not be possible to find land which is not cultivated at present, which is useless, but which might become, after

trees are planted and the forest improved, a normal area in 15, 20 or 30 years.
If one visits the provinces, one can see land which has been cleared for several years and has no value today. If, at the time of this study on tree planting it was decided to plant trees on this land, it would have a much greater value in a few years. This would also provide a livelihood for the farmers of the area, who would help those organizations in this work.
The second point I wish to deal with briefly before the opening of this federal-provincial conference is the following: We hear more and more about the extension of farms.
Mr. Chairman, it is correct that, in certain areas, the farmer must be encouraged to enlarge his farm. But the fact of increasing the size of a farm does not necessarily mean larger incomes.
At a public meeting, I said that in Ontario and Quebec between 55 and 60 per cent of dairy producers had less than 13 milk cows. Now, after the meeting I met an economist who told me: "The only way for those dairy farmers to double their income is to have 26 cows instead of 13".
Mr. Chairman, it is not that easy because, as I said before in this house, it is possible to have a net income of $3,000 with 58 milk cows, and it is also possible to have a net income of $3,000 a year with only 18 milk cows.
It all depends on the equipment the farmer has and on the efficiency of his production. We must not limit ourselves to the expansion of farms or the greater number of acres; most important of all, we must give special consideration to the productivity of every acre of land owned by a farmer and to the efficiency of his farm equipment and cattle before advising him to increase his acreage or his cattle substantially.
A man who is not too well-informed and who does not work so very hard on a small or on an average farm has little chance of increasing his income by just adding to his acreage. It is easy to understand why. The fact that a man owns a larger farm does not increase his know-how.
Mr. Chairman, this brings me to speak of the technical assistance that provincial governments can provide for the farmers in our districts.
According to the agreements entered into with the provinces under ARDA, the federal government pays half the cost of any project. I am convinced that if provincial governments, following the agreements to be signed
Interim Supply
early in 1965, would provide for our farmers the technical assistance they need to cultivate their farm or to increase the output of the land they own today, just like the bank manager helps the owner of a business concern to start operating, 1 am convinced, that it would be a good step forward to help eastern farmers.
Mr. Chairman, while travelling through our ridings, our province and other Canadian provinces, we meet some farmers who manage to earn a decent living from their farm and we ask them how they manage to do that.
What occurs generally is that a family head has two or three of his sons who are farmers and who live near by. These farmers-his sons-share in a family corporation the same agricultural machines, the same tractors, the same hay-press, the same tools.
Allow me to give you an example. There is in my riding a farmer who has three sons living in the neighbourhood. He told me he had purchased a combined sowing machine for which he had paid $850. This combined sowing machine is used on an average farm about half a day in a year. For the average farmer, the price of such a machine is prohibitive compared to the service it gives. But if this family head who has purchased such a machine shares it with two or three of his sons, this allows them to reduce their production cost and realize a greater net profit.
If this exists in family corporations, why should the federal government, in conjunction with the provincial governments, not organize what we used to have in the past, the so-called farming circles, where farmers, by means of a corporation or a union, got together, using the same machines and the same tools? Their production costs were thus reduced by half.
That is, in my opinion, part of the technical assistance-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time is over.
Mr. Chairman, like other members on this side of the chamber I am concerned about the excessive expenditures of the government.
I am sure you are.
Thank you.
Especially P.F.A.A.

I am one of those hon. members who believe the main duty of the opposition is to examine the estimates of the

Interim Supply
government and scrutinize the expenditures. The government has not given us the opportunity to do so. In fact, it has dragged a red herring across our path in the name of the flag.
At the moment I am concerned with the cost of a picayune inquiry instigated by the flippant remark passed by an inexperienced minister of the crown. I wonder how much this inquiry cost the Canadian people. Reference was made in the press today to this inquiry. It called it a judicial inquiry and said it was a judicial report that was laid down.
I contend that it was not a judicial report, that it was a political report, and I am surprised that any judge, knowing the political overtones of an inquiry of this sort, would jeopardize the independence of the judiciary by acting as a judge in this connection, if not for some reason as yet unrevealed.
Shame.
You wait until I am finished and you will see the shame.
It hurts too much. They can't take it.

I would say it is a political report for more than one reason. Maybe the members of the committee do not know this, but I am informed that the judge who presided as commissioner, not in the capacity of judge but as commissioner, was a defeated Liberal candidate in the city of Moose Jaw. Not only that, his counsel, who acted for the government, was a defeated nominee for the candidacy of the Liberal party, and the second lawyer who acted for the government on behalf of the P.F.A.A. was a chief fund raiser for the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan for a number of years, and was chairman of the finance committee.
Another person who should have been connected with this, but who was not called by this, as I say, political commissioner, was the liaison officer who worked between the director and the minister. I say that he should have been called because he had some doing in the dismissal of one of my constituents. I ask why did the commissioner not go into this phase of it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw your attention to citations 149(j) and 152(4) in Beauchesne's fourth edition, concerning the unparliamentary practice of referring to judges.
But he is a Grit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I would like to refer to citation 149(j) which says:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 35; it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
(j) cast reflections upon the conduct of judges of superior courts, unless such conduct is based upon a substantive motion-
All references to judges and courts of justice and to personages of high official station of the nature of personal attack and censure, have always been considered unparliamentary and the Speakers of the British and Canadian houses have always treated them as breaches of order.
I would ask, Mr. Chairman, that you would rule on this particular point of order and, if you saw fit, discourage any further such references.
I would suggest there is no point of order-

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think we all appreciate what the hon. member said about references to judges, but surely when judges are merely acting as commissioners they are no more immune from comment than any other individual would happen to be. I wonder if the hon. member who has raised this point of order would say whether these citations carry to the extent that a judge appointed to a specific job as commissioner is free from any comment in this chamber?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: If I might answer that, the second quotation refers to an attack on or censure of a judge in his office of judge, no matter in what capacity he is acting, in any judicial proceeding. I would submit that the inquiry to which the hon. member was referring was a judicial proceeding.

I suggest, there is no point of order, because the citation the hon. member mentioned referred to superior court judges, and the judge I am referring to is a county court judge, or what we in the west say is a district court judge, and if this person had acted in the manner a judge should act I would not be making these remarks.
He is not here to defend himself.
That is right, but neither was my constituent when your minister made the accusation. The judge is surely capable of defending himself and I will give him every opportunity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. Is the hon. member rising on a point of order?
I am only replying to the hon. member's invitation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order please. The point of order which has been raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is of interest to all hon. members, and I know that the hon. member who has the floor now wants to take into account the reference made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George to citations 149(j) and 152(4) in Beauchesne's.
I admit there is obviously a distinction between a judge who acts in his strict judicial capacity and a judge who, in a circumstance such as this one, is acting not in a strict judicial capacity but rather as a commissioner of inquiry. However, I do not think this permits the hon. member to attack and make inferences against the judge in a personal way. I think he is in order if he refers to him in his official capacity as a commissioner, and if the hon. member, who I believe has just about completed his remarks in connection with the judgment of the judge, will limit his remarks to this particular aspect then there should be no problem. I hope the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George will agree that this is the way we should look at the problem.

With all deference to your remarks, Mr. Chairman, I am not a lawyer but I understand that in the Judges Act power is given to parliament, the Senate and the House of Commons, to call judges to order at any time. In fact, the only action the Canadian people can take is through the parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is on a substantive motion, if any hon. member wants to make a substantive motion; but the rules provide that it is only under that particular circumstance that parliament can take a judge, whether a judge of the superior courts, or county or district courts, to task. It has to be done by substantive motion and it is not my understanding that this is what the hon. member wants to do.

If that is your ruling I will bow to it. In future I shall refer to him as the commissioner, but you all know whom I mean. I have the evidence taken by this commissioner, a commissioner appointed by the
Interim Supply
government-and I refer to the connection of this legal official-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
When I have finished. Sit down.
Oh, oh.

I think back to 1963 when the hon. member who just got up asked a lot of trivial questions. I am trying to establish that one of the witnesses should have been called. I also wish to establish at the same time that one of the witnesses upon which this commissioner relies so much did not give the right facts while under oath.
Oh, oh.

Just a minute. On page 852- I will quote some of this-a question was asked of the witness: "Are you required from time to time to submit reports on your supervisors?" The witness said in reply-and here, perhaps, I will read without interruption the series of questions and answers:
A. There is an efficiency rating in connection with various employees in the services, and that report is signed by the employee and superintendent in the case of the supervisors and is signed by myself.
Q. To whom do these reports go?
A. They come to Ottawa.
Q. You send them on to the minister?
A. They are sent on to the minister. They are sent on through to the administration in Ottawa. This is particularly in a case where there are increments in salary coming to the employee. His efficiency report is completed at that time with remarks attached to it.
Q. Prior to your submitting the report, to which the minister has referred in the house, did you discuss the subject with anyone else?
A. Discuss what?
Q. Mr. Walker's dismissal or the procedure in respect of how to go about it?
A. X cannot say that I discussed the matter of his dismissal with anyone else. I took it upon myself to write a letter to the deputy minister in connection with it.
Q. Without any advice?
A. That is my prerogative as director.
Q. I do not deny that. I am just asking you the question, yes or no. You have answered no, you did not discuss it with anyone.
A. No, I did not discuss it with anyone.
The next morning, as members of that committee will recall, this same witness came in and asked permission to change his testimony. He said he did discuss it with someone else, and hon. members seated in this committee will well remember that.
I am alarmed when a Canadian who holds the position which this commissioner holds in our judiciary in Canada should allow

Interim Supply
himself to submit a report like the one submitted to this house yesterday. Before I go into this further, perhaps I should make my position in this matter perfectly clear. I think my position is very similar to that of all other hon. members. I say that an elected member of parliament is a representative and spokesman for his constituency in regard to federal matters. I feel it is my duty to protect the rightful interests and entitlements of my constituents at all times, both individually and as a group. Now in this issue, it appears to me that two major questions were involved. The first was the delayed payment by the department of 1962 P.F.A.A. awards to farmers in the Swift Current area. Second was the suspicion on the part of the P.F.A.A. director of a "fix"-this was the term the director himself used when evidence was given before the commissioner. I heard it myself and it will be found recorded in the transcript of evidence which the commissioner has. With regard to the delayed payments-and I want all members of the committee to note this-clause 7 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act states:
Every award authorized under this act shall be paid in the month of December.
This inquiry took place because I was insisting that my farmers were not being paid until March, three months after they should have been paid. Also in the act is a paragraph headed "Offences and Penalties" which states:
Every person is guilty of an offence under this Act and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars who
(a) violates or fails to comply with any provision of this act or any regulation;
I also ask members of this committee to pay particular attention to the word "shall". The act says these payments "shall" be paid in the month of December. I say that the act is the law of our country and that no person, not even a minister of the crown, can overrule its provisions. But in spite of this knowledge, the director of his own accord did withhold payment with respect to a number of townships in my constituency. There were roughly 54 townships from which payments were withheld and the number of farmers affected was roughly 1,000. The reason given by the director for withholding payment even though the awards had been authorized by the board of review was that he was suspicious because he had received a letter from one farmer complaining about his neighbours. There was no foundation for the complaint and subsequent evidence revealed this to be a fact. There is no evidence in the judge's

report that there were any irregularities of any kind, and I intend to prove this later.
As the federal member of parliament representing these farmers I demanded that payment be made according to the act unless evidence could be produced that its provisions had been violated. No such evidence was produced so I made further demands stating again that no person, certainly not the director or members of the board of review, had the power to withhold payment of the legitimate claims of farmers if their claims had been passed for payment. I pointed out that if it were later proven that there had been a violation of the act there were several methods of recovery which could be adopted by the administrative branch of the department, namely, either by due process of law or by setting up an overpayment account, as has been done in the past in other parts of western Canada.
On no occasion did I object to an investigation being carried out in this area if it were deemed necessary and if any proof were presented that there were any irregularities. However, as I have previously stated no specific cases were presented, and as a result no investigation has been held. None has ever been held. No inquiry was held even after this government had been in office for a number of months. I wonder why, if there was any foundation for a charge that irregularities had occurred.
I have referred already to the word "fix" which was used by the director at the hearing of evidence before this commissioner. He, personally, must have gone through 8,000 applications. On this basis he presented four charges-four applications which, he suggested, were "fixed" and these are referred to in this report by the commissioner. I wish to refer to one of them and I will use the name, as I must, because it appears in any case in the report. It is the case of a young farmer by the name of Bymoen. He made a claim for P.F.A.A. assistance. Such cases occur quite often; there is nothing irregular about this. This young man made a claim for P.F.A.A. payments to which he was entitled. On investigation the Regina office, through the director, said he did not lease the land. No trouble was taken to investigate-like the supervisor-but when an investigation was completed, it was found that this was what had happened: The lad had recently got married and his father-in-law was going to assist him to set up farming. He made an application to the farm credit board for a sum of money to purchase a parcel of land which he

planned to farm. But as members of this committee know, it takes a considerable time for these applications to be processed and in the meantime the person from whom he intended to purchase the land decided to farm it once more. This left the young lad in a difficulty. However, his father-in-law said: Don't worry about it; I will lease you some of my own land so that you can go ahead and farm.
In the part he had leased to his son-in-law was a quarter section of land he had leased from another person. The lease was in the father-in-law's name. There was a verbal lease between the son-in-law and the father-in-law, which is quite permissible out there under the P.F.A.A. regulations, for the first year. However, the director said this was a fix, until we proved otherwise. The commissioner took no notice, apparently, judging from his report, of the facts that were presented to him at the hearings. I wonder why.
Another reference to one of the cases that was called a fix by the director is in regard to a piece of irrigated land. For those who know anything about P.F.A.A., any land that is irrigated is taken out of the area for which P.F.A.A. is paid and the average of that area is figured out without the production from the irrigated land. This irrigation was not the same as other types of irrigation we have out there; it was what we call a spring flood irrigation, and was quite legitimate. I am surprised that the commissioner says this.
Carried.

Here he is talking about the dismissal of Mr. Walker. He says:
Here possibly I should review some of the matters that were placed before the commission, which although perhaps small in themselves, caused some apprehension in the mind of the director in his dealings with him.
"Small in themselves". This is the type of statement he makes in regard to Mr. Walker all through his report. He finally comes up with a decision in which he says it was necessary and desirable that Mr. Walker be relieved of his duties. I suggest that it was necessary and desirable as far as this commissioner was concerned because the commissioner was a supporter of the Liberal party and Mr. Walker was a supporter of the Tory party.
Oh, oh.

That was the only reason. There was no other reason why he should have been dismissed. I would also like to

refer to other statements the commissioner has made in his report, which statements are very misleading. In fact, he has made reference to some evidence that I gave before the inquiry. It is not necessary that I read all this to the committee, but this evidence was in connection with an interview I had with the director. The director came to see me in my office and his opening remarks were, "McIntosh, you are not running the P.F.A.A. in Swift Current. I am the director; I am running P.F.A.A. here". I said, "Mr. Riddell, you have made some accurate statements, and others that are not quite accurate." I said, "In the first place, you are right; I am not running P.F.A.A. You are the director; you are correct in that statement. But in regard to your running P.F.A.A., you are wrong". And that is where the evidence stops in this report. Why did the judge not complete the statement that I made, when I said, "You are not running P.F.A.A.; the Minister of Agriculture is running P.F.A.A."?
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member has just said, "Why did the judge stop at this point?" I thought he was going to call him the commissioner while he was speaking tonight.

I thank my hon. friend for that correction, Mr. Chairman. If I forget again, I hope you will remind me. I also refer to another page of testimony, I guess you could call it, that I gave at the inquiry. The lawyer was asking me if I knew a certain person. I said:
Very well. When I went into the Skyline hotel I asked if Mr.-
-so-and-so:
-was there, and I was directed to a room upstairs to which I went. I knocked and went in, and there were several gentlemen in the room. I immediately recognized them as members of the board of review. I said, "What is this, an official or unofficial visit?" They said it was an unofficial visit. I said, "In what respect?" They said, "In connection with the holding back of payments on the P.F.A.A. cheques". I said, "On what grounds?" I was informed that because of the suspicions of Mr. Riddell. I asked, "What suspicions did Mr. Riddell have?" They said something to do with the carryover of wheat in particular areas. I said, "Gentlemen, those are suspicions. Has he given you any concrete examples of whether there are irregularities in any of these areas?" They said, "No, he hadn't at that time". I talked with them again for close to an hour and in this field, and I also talked about politics-
Which the commissioner did not wish me to get into. Then I said:
However, I must make this statement, that I was afraid that there was political influence being used in this case-

Interim Supply
Because these payments were withheld in my area just before an election. Why were they withheld? On whose orders were they withheld? I wanted to know. I said:
-I reminded them of a former instance where it seemed to me that politics were creeping in and what had happened the individual concerned was the former director-
This was the person whom I referred to earlier as the liaison officer between the present director and the minister at the time:
I told them further that if they had no concrete examples and they had passed these claims, then they had no authority to withhold the cheques. I think I cited the act. I told them that the cheques should have gone out in December and if they insisted that they had the power to withhold, then possibly the penalty provisions within the act should be applied; that they were violating the act if they were using that type of power, which they had no authority to do.
I also informed them that this was an act passed by the parliament of Canada and once it was passed it applied to everyone; not even the minister could violate the provisions of it without the penalty being applied if someone so wished, and in this case, I so wished, on behalf of the people that I represented. And if I was going to have any more trouble with this, I would lay a complaint against the whole works, including the director, the board of review or anybody else that tried to interfere in withholding these cheques.
I presume this is where the commission got the charge that appears in the paper, that I had threatened Mr. Riddell and the P.F.A.A. board of review. Well, if that is so, I would have done it with regard to anyone who was withholding cheques from my constituents, and I am quite sure anyone in this House of Commons would have done the same thing.
Hear, hear.

I just want to refer to one more statement in regard to Mr. Walker. The commissioner in the report says that he should have been dismissed. He says that Mr. Walker "was caught in the middle of a controversy between Mr. Riddell and Mr. McIntosh", and because he was caught in the middle, the commissioner stated he should have been fired. This is another passage. The commissioner said:
I can, of course, understand Mr. McIntosh's reluctance, as a member of parliament running for office, to have any investigation concerning anything within his constituency. But I cannot understand Mr. McIntosh's lack of understanding with respect to the obligations of Mr. Riddell, as director, to make sure that nothing improper was being done by claimants under the act, nor can I understand the position taken by Mr. Walker in regard to this controversy.
One of the reasons why he cannot understand, perhaps, is because he is a defeated

candidate and I am a successful one. Maybe he should follow my methods.
Further, he goes on to say that there may have been a misunderstanding in respect to the instructions which Mr. Walker received from Mr. Riddell in this regard; but it is hard to see how there can be any misunderstanding. There may have been one, but it is hard to see where there is one.
Another statement by the commissioner which I question is with regard to the inspectors who were employed. He said that many of them did not attempt to obtain accurate information. These inspectors are very honest men. That is one of the reasons they are selected for this position, and for any commissioner to make that accusation with the evidence which he had at his disposal at the inquiry is an affront to the position he holds. I am alarmed that a man holding such a position should make a statement which he knew would be publicized in this way. It is too bad that we have not some recourse within our country which would enable a person like that, to use an actor's phrase, to be brought on the carpet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member's time has expired, unless he has unanimous consent to continue.
No.

Mr. Chairman, I was interrupted for a couple of minutes but I will close off by saying this. My immediate reaction to the commissioner's conclusion can be summed up in the phrase: "Suppressio veri et suggestio falsi", which as most hon. members know means "Suppression of the truth and suggestion of the false." Had the commissioner delivered these conclusions in his capacity as a judge prior to accepting the commission I would have taken action in this house to have him removed from that position; but because he delivered these conclusions under the cover given to a commissioner by the government I am left without any remedy against him.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit the question I was going to
ask?
