Mr. Chairman, while the committee is in the process of dealing with the very important subject of interim supply, which is asking us to approve expenditures in excess of $700 million, I should like to make a few brief remarks in relation to the

Department of Forestry, mainly relating to the agreements between the federal government and the provinces on shared programs.
I should like to mention at the outset that the committee were very interested to hear the remarks yesterday made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton in outlining the functions of the department, the department of which incidentally the hon. member was the first minister. It is interesting to note that this department, which has been discussed both yesterday and today, came into being under the guidance of the former administration. When you look into many of the programs which the department is carrying out at the present time, you find more and more that a great deal of tribute can be paid to the former administration for bringing these programs into being. Yesterday the former minister gave us a very detailed account of the functions of the Department of Forestry and summarized the extent of our forestry resources, as well as giving a general picture of the present value of exports of raw and finished materials. I was also pleased to hear of the co-operation of a financial nature which is taking place between the federal government and the provinces under this particular department. It is extremely important that these programs be continued, and as quickly as possible improved.
Although I note that some small increases are planned in the Department of Forestry in relation to certain research programs of the department-and here I might say that it is interesting to see that increases in expenditures are going to be made in regard to research into this very important subject- I also observe that there has been no increase in relation to the contributions to the provinces in regard to the conducting of forestry inventories, reforestation, forest fire protection and forest access road construction, a fact which I am disturbed to learn. These programs are some of the most important ones, and they must not only be continued but carried out on a much larger scale. I sincerely hope that the government will give early consideration to working out details with the provinces which will result in greater contributions on the part of the federal government toward these very desirable projects.
In dealing with payments to the provinces, I have some brief remarks to make in relation to the particular forestry situation, forestry programs and potential in the province of Manitoba. I will refer at times to the re-
Interim Supply
port of the committee on Manitoba's economic future, which is quite a voluminous report. However, I intend only to refer to certain parts of it. Although the forestry resources of the provinces actually come under the jurisdiction of the provinces themselves, the absolute necessity for co-operation between the federal government and the provincial authorities is very apparent as one looks over some of the findings of the committee which presented this report to the Manitoba government in March, 1963. The report starts out by saying that the primary forest resources of Manitoba, while not as highly productive as those of British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec, and more remote from major markets, nevertheless offer great potential for development and utilization. The annual value of products extracted by the primary forest industries of Manitoba is approximately $20 million. The major products are newsprint, pulpwood, sawn lumber, poles, posts, crossties and fuel wood. Pulp and paper products, including newsprint, account for 90 per cent of the total value of all woods harvested. About one third is exported from the province as pulpwood. A large portion of the remainder is manufactured into newsprint. There is a pulp and paper plant at Pine Falls, Manitoba which, incidentally, at the moment is the only pulp and paper plant we have in that province.
The report goes on to say that some of these shared programs are extremely valuable and very necessary. The report deals with many things such as access roads and power development. It is interesting to note when we speak of power development that Premier Roblin of Manitoba, when making a statement to the legislature on February 21, 1962, mentioned power specifically and underlined the fact that it would open up unlimited possibilities for growth in northern Manitoba, and that it would provide for the development of provincial resources that otherwise might remain undeveloped for many years. It is very important, you will note, to continue the development of access roads in order to ensure future development of our forestry resources in all the provinces, including Manitoba.
You might wonder why I am associating the development of power sites with the subject of forestry. Here again we have a shared service, in some respects. When speaking of these shared services, it is interesting to note how many of them were originally instituted by the former administration. I mentioned access roads. The program to develop access roads was closely associated

Interim Supply
with the roads to resources program which, in many respects, serve the same purpose. We know that the roads to resources program is one which the present Prime Minister referred to at one time as nothing but roads from igloo to igloo. This program is working out very well in many parts of Canada. I imagine the Prime Minister will always regret the time he made that statement. I hope, although there is not much evidence as yet, that he has changed his mind about this program.
Getting back to the shared programs and power development, it is interesting to look at the announcement recently made by the present government, and which is a followup of a program entered into by the province of Manitoba and the government of Canada, relating to a study of the power potential of the Nelson river. A month or so ago this government announced that further studies would be continued under this same agreement. I can say that we in Manitoba are very pleased to see the present government continuing programs instituted by the previous administration.
I have pointed out that in relation to forestry development and the development of the forest industry in Manitoba, it is essential that we have not only power developed as rapidly as we can but that we also have access roads into our forest areas. Assistance to the development of access roads is one of the functions of the Department of Forestry.
I should like to mention also that the benefits of forestry research are almost unlimited and the necessity for newer and improved methods of assessing forest products potential are continually being improved. For example, in Manitoba we find-actually this relates to one of the functions of the federal Department of Forestry-the province is being assisted in setting up forest inventory. The report states that the estimate of timber resources in the province of Manitoba made in the thirties, upon which the existing forestry policy of the province was based, indicated that the annual drain from logging, fires, insects and disease exceeded the annual growth. This was an estimate made in the thirties. A much more comprehensive inventory just completed shows the earlier estimate to have been seriously wrong. It is now considered that accessible crown land alone will sustain an annual cut of almost 100 million cubic feet of softwood, and it is possible that even this estimate is conservative. However the total cut of wood for the province has tended to decline of late and the average for

five recent years has been only 34 million cubic feet of all species from crown lands. This shows that new inventories are not only desirable but a necessity.
The federal Department of Forestry should provide more improved methods for conducting inventories from time to time, as I am sure these improved methods are being developed. Dealing again with the forestry potential of Manitoba, the report states it is estimated that the consumption of lumber in Manitoba is at least four or five times the present level of production. Production, which is presently being carried out by many small sawmills, could be improved upon tremendously through the good offices and the assistance of the federal Department of Forestry. It is estimated, the report says, that upwards of 150 million board feet of lumber could be produced and sold annually in the province by 12 to 15 saw mills instead of the present 40 million board feet produced by over 200 saw mills. The report indicates, therefore, that we have many small saw mills operating today which could be operating far more efficiently if they had encouragement and if more information were forthcoming from the federal department.
I could go on for an indefinite period of time dealing with the findings of the report on Manitoba's economic future in relation to the forest industry alone. The report indicates that there is opportunity in northern Manitoba to establish, over an eight to 10 year period, a pulpwood cutting and debarking operation for spruce pulpwood for sale in the overseas market, with shipment going through the port of Churchill. Substantial quantities could be cut and exported without depleting any of these pulpwood forests. Here again, we can see the tremendous advantage in continually conducting forest inventories. I should like to see that under the guidance of the Minister of Forestry.
There are only one or two further brief comments I have to make. We also have the ARDA program. We in western Canada hope it will not be too long until the ARDA program is rapidly extended in the western prairies. I would also hope that it will not be too long before the minister will embark on a program of using the possibilities available under ARDA in relation to Indian reservations. I believe that here is a great opportunity for expansion of the program. I might say here that the ARDA program was brought into being under the former administration, so once again we

are quite happy to note that the present government is continuing a program instituted by the former administration.
I should like to suggest as strongly as I can to the minister through the acting minister that the fullest consideration be given to *entering into a program under ARDA on Indian reservations. I think there is a vast field here where this program could operate to the benefit of our first citizens. I hope the minister will look into this possibility and make an announcement in the near future.
Before leaving the Department of Forestry I should once again like to pay tribute to the wonderful and highly creditable work being done by the forest products research branch on the Montreal road. All of us should take the opportunity to visit this project as often as we can. I have only had the opportunity of being there once but I can assure all hon. members that a visit to the forest products research branch is most interesting, revealing and educational. I am sure the work they are doing will enable Canada not only to hold its competitive position in the sale of forest products in world markets but will assist Canada to expand her present markets very rapidly. At the present time Canada is in competition with the world in this regard. The only way we can maintain or increase our markets is by producing a better product. This is one of the goals toward which the forest products research branch on the Montreal road is working day by day. I think all of us owe them a great debt of gratitude.

Mr. Chairman, as I do not want to interrupt the filibuster which is being carried out by the Conservatives who are anxious to prevent the debate on the flag from taking place, I shall refrain from speaking.

Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as I come from the prairies it may surprise hon. members that I should speak on forestry, but I want to point out just how important trees are to the prairies and the fact that they can be grown there. In the 1930's a program was started in Saskatchewan of planting hedges in the fields and trees on the farms as weather belts. The program was carried out at the little town of Conquest in the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar. The farmers started a hedge growing program to stop the soil from blowing away and to afford protection against high winds. Today
Interim Supply
Conquest can boast of a thousand miles of hedges. These hedges were planted around the edges of the fields 160 rods apart and extended a full mile. They beautified the country and it was not very long before their ability to prevent erosion was seen. In the wintertime the hedges prevent heavy drifting caused by blowing snow. They have resulted in the government being able to save a lot of money in keeping roads open in the winter and also holding the snow on the land, which is very important from the point of view of the moisture that western Canada needs so much. I suggest that the minister speed up the tree planting program on the prairies as it is certainly needed.
In the northern part of the province we have forests but they are being logged off. The same thing happened in Ontario where the hardwood trees were cut down and milled. After 100 years Ontario is beginning to realize the importance of trees and forests and is starting a farm woodlot program.
The forestry farm in Saskatoon is one of the beauty spots of Saskatchewan, but we must have water to grow trees and make the prairies blossom. The Saskatchewan river dam will be finished in a couple of years. It will then take a few years to fill up the reservoirs but when that happens we will have the water for this program. We should not slash down and log off our forests in northern Saskatchewan in the way that Ontario logged off its timber 100 years ago, and now has to undertake a tree lot program. Where trees are being logged off in northern Saskachewan I think replanting of trees should be done now. I suggest to the minister that he should look into this matter. It all comes under the ARDA program, but I feel that somewhere along the line the people in charge of the program are dragging their feet. It is not going ahead on the prairies as fast as I should like to see it proceed.
We are short of community pastures on the prairies and I believe this program should be speeded up by putting large tracts of land into community pastures and at the same time planting trees for shade. When that country was opened the land should never have been broken up, and we are beginning to realize that now. It is the same thing in the north where they are cutting timber, clearing off the land, when instead much of the land should be left as forest.
On the prairies I would like to see the ARDA program speeded up to take land out of production and put it into better use as pasture. We have a big cattle industry in

Interim Supply
Saskatchewan. In the 1930's our farmers were caught without feed, but we are overcoming that problem now. Our biggest difficulty is that the cattle industry has been hampered by lack of sufficient summer pasture, and I am glad to see ARDA is providing more pastures because when we have them we will be able to breed a lot more quality cattle.
The same thing applies to the north. Pastures could be developed in the bush and, if they were, they would be very valuable assets to the province of Saskatchewan. I had not intended to speak at length but I hope the minister will give consideration to the suggestions I have made for speeding up the ARDA program and accelerating tree planting on the prairies. Some place along the line I feel someone is dragging his feet.
The Saskatchewan river dam will be finished in a couple of years and then we will have water to irrigate pastures, which will add greatly to the economy of the province.

Mr. Chairman, as it has been said in sensible newspapers, I do not want to be associated with that kind of filibuster set up by the Conservatives. And, especially, I do not want to delay the adoption of the Canadian flag. Consequently, I will not make the speech I intended to make tonight.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in the debate on the interim supply bill which is now before us, I feel I am facing my responsibilities in seeking to scrutinize the expenditures made by the government.
We just saw two Liberal members rising to say they did not intend to take part in the debate. There is nothing new in that, Mr. Chairman, because they decided to maintain a stubborn silence and follow the decisions and the discipline of the party requiring that they say nothing. If this is their tactics, their policy, to enter into an agreement and co-operate with the splinter parties in order to gloss over expenditures of $700 million, it is their business, but my colleagues of the Conservative party and myself have a responsibility towards the people and if we are rising to speak, it is not to obstruct but to seek information and because we want to see that the government expenditures are well controlled.
We have before us a request to pass-
Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question?
When I have finished my remarks, I shall be pleased to answer, as always.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) is now sitting in the press gallery where he is not supposed to be. He should be sitting in his seat. I think this is an insult to our distinguished journalists and he should be sitting in the comer over there.

On two occasions we have been charged with obstruction. I should like to point out to the house that, yesterday, three members of the New Democratic party and one from the Ralliement Creditiste took part in our proceedings and I am told that today the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste also made a speech.
I say again that if hon. members opposite are not responsible enough to take their mandate seriously, they alone will have to take the consequences. They ought not to rise in this chamber and try to make mountains out of molehills.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is suggesting that members on this side of the chamber are not fulfilling their duties by not participating in this debate. I would like to point out that the hon. member was not present when the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources were being discussed last Friday.

Mr. Chairman, if you can see any justification for the remark of my hon. friend you are much better than I am. 1 think he just stood up in his place to make an appearance, in order that the press gallery would take a note of it and put some writeup in the Toronto newspapers.

As I was saying a moment ago, it is our responsibility and our duty to examine thoroughly government expenditures. We tried on many occasions to obtain answers, but it is clear that the government does not intend to provide us with the information we are requesting.
We have obvious proof of this when we realize that during the consideration of supplementary estimates of a department in particular, the minister in charge of that department is not even in attendance to answer questions.
He is on the isle of Capri.

He is holidaying. I am speaking more particularly of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) who is joy riding in Europe when he should be here answering questions we want to put to him.
There you have further evidence, Mr. Chairman, of the lack of interest, the jauntiness and the arrogance of the members of the present cabinet.
For instance, may I draw your attention to the fact that, at today's sitting, there has never been more than four ministers, out of 25, in attendance in the house.
They are working.

They are working. They are in Europe, enjoying themselves. They are not working, they are holidaying in Europe. That is the kind of work these wartime administrators can do: go to Europe and get a suntan on the shores of the Mediterranean.
Up until now, Mr. Chairman, nine days have been spent on studying the estimates of the various departments. In an ordinary year, on the same date, the same number of days have in general been spent on studying government's expenditures.
Where is the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton)?

Mr. Chairman, it is well and good for the ministers to spend the people's money like drunken sailors as they are now doing but the members of the opposition have to examine such expenditures closely and make sure that they are made within the law. And that is one reason for my intervention in this debate.
When the hon. members opposite say that we are filibustering, I tell them that if they consider our participation in the debate on Bill No. C-110 as a filibuster-
It was division.

-I am glad I went in for filibustering tactics, because, with the help of my colleagues of the Conservative party, we managed to correct a piece of legislation full of deficiencies and totally against the interest of the Canadian people.
On many instances, I tried to get information from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) with regard to the projects he had in mind to give work to the Canadian unemployed and more especially those in Quebec.
In the province of Quebec we have the dubious honour of holding the unemployment record in Canada, because at the present time there are 105,000 unemployed, the majority of whom are family heads.
Interim Supply
Are there some unemployed with a job?

Mr. Chairman, these jobless people would like to work but they cannot find any work, because this government is unable to offer projects which could provide work for those who are looking for employment.
On several occasions, I asked the Minister of Labour what plans he had in mind and I never could get the required information. I intended to avail myself of this debate to ask him again what were his plans to give jobs to the unemployed in the province of Quebec, but I notice he is absent as usual.
Mr. Chairman, we remember the high sounding speeches made by my hon. friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin)-he left the house a few moments ago-when he sat on this side. In fact, he enjoyed the pleasure-*
Lustful.

-of asking and repeating questions to the then minister of labour to know what he was doing to find jobs for this or that dozen of unemployed who had just been dismissed in an industry. But since he has been sitting to your right, no one has seen the Secretary of State for External Affairs tackle the problem of finding jobs for our unemployed with as much eagerness as he did when he sat on this side of the house.
The problem is settled.

Mr. Chairman, I hear the hon. member for Longueuil say that the problem is settled. Although there are 105,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec, they consider that the problem has been settled, it would not be worthwhile to take the time of the house or make representations to the Minister of Labour in order to give those hungry unemployed the bread needed by them and their families.
But when they sat on this side of the house it was an obsession with them, and day after day they asked questions concerning unemployment and the steps that had to be taken to hold it in check.
Mr. Chairman, you will remember that at one time the then member for Laurier-
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to note that my friends opposite are applauding my remarks to the effect that the former member for Laurier has now left the house

Interim Supply
because I understand that they had some difficulty in making him accept their views. When I named him in this house, they heartily applauded, because they are happy that he is no longer among them.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I recognized that it is a slip of the tongue on the part of the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, but since his remarks will be put on the record, I wish to make a correction.
The hon. member said: "I am glad to see that my friends opposite are applauding at the fact that the former member for Laurier has gone out". Mr. Chairman, I think that such words are improper and uncalled for. We have applauded the name of the former member for Laurier because he is a French Canadian who has always done credit to us.
There is no point of order. Do learn the standing orders.

Mr. Chairman, like you, I forgave in advance the little knowledge that the hon. member for Lotbiniere possesses in regard to the standing orders. Like you, I also understood that as he is here only a few times a month, he cannot have had the opportunity to-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The remarks just made by the hon. member are entirely unfair. I am regularly in attendance in the House of Commons and I shall even say that I am steadier than the hon. members for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) who are both absent, as well as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. May I remind the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot that it is contrary to the rules to refer to the absence or the presence of certain members, and I would ask the hon. member to please limit his remarks to the matter presently before us.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Was the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Lotbiniere in accordance with the standing orders?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must say the question of privilege was out of order, but we have disposed of it.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lotbiniere should learn the rules; he should go back to school.

The hon. member for
Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is ignorant and stupid.

I said a moment ago that the unemployment situation was alarming, especially in the province of Quebec, where there are still 105,000 jobless. We had the right to expect that unemployment would be wiped out, since those who are now on the government side had promised full employment during their election campaigns of 1962 and 1963.
However, Mr. Chairman, you can compare the number of unemployed in April, May, June, July, August and September 1962 with the corresponding months in 1963. You will then agree with me that there has been very little change.
I will quote first the figures for 1962:
April, 171,000; May, 114,000; June, 105,000; July, 109,000; August, 96,000; September, 97,000.
I will now give the figures for 1963:
April, 182,000; May, 130,000; June, 113,000; July, 112,000; August, 108,000; September, 108,000.
Where are the hundreds of jobs which our hon. friends opposite were supposed to find for the unemployed in the province of Quebec?
To speak about a matter in which I am greatly interested, I will quote the figures given me by the local unemployment insurance office in St. Hyacinthe. According to these figures, there were 1,310 applications for jobs in the month of June; in May, there were 1,414; in April, 2,094, in March, 2,577, in February, 2,470. In January, there were 2,344.
Those are unemployed to whom the Liberals had promised jobs.
They do not have a good member.
I just heard my hon. friend from Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) interrupt to say that my constituency does not have a good member. I should like to reply-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I did not say that his constituency did not have a good member. I put this as a question: "Would it not have, by any chance, a member who is not doing a good job?"
I was just asking.
To answer my hon. friend, I would remind him that the person now speaking had obtained-
A portfolio.
I did not hear that remark.
He obtained a portfolio.

I understand why some hon. members opposite can say: "The grapes are sour".
I had obtained the building of a penitentiary, but the great patriot, to whom my hon. friend from Lotbiniere referred to a moment ago lost no time in cancelling the project out of political partisanship-
That is not true.

Hon. Lionel Chevrier cancelled the building of that penitentiary after it had been decided to go ahead with it.
The decision was taken purely for political reasons. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do; and those around him know it too.
The St. Sylvestre station is also closed; you are pretty cheap.

Last Friday, the Minister of Forestry read a press release on the temporary policy of the government regarding feed grain.
The reading of that news release proved to us that the present government is entirely incapable of solving once for all the problem of feed grain, in spite of the fact that it had promised to do so during the election campaign.
It was also proved to us without the shadow of a doubt that the Minister of Forestry, who is responsible for the matter of feed grain, was speaking of something he did not know anything about.
Mr. Chairman, if you refer to the press release, you will note that the freight subsidy would amount to $1.30 and the balance payable by the breeders would range up to $6.20.
It also says:
Under the new policy, that difference of approximately $B was reduced to $2.60 in eastern Canada and it is expected that the competition from trucking firms will eventually reduce that margin to less than $1.60.
What is it all about, Mr. Chairman?
Are we talking about subsidies on 100 pounds, a ton, a wagonload or a shipload of grain?
I am told that when newspapermen got that release they were panicky, because nobody understood anything. The Minister of Forestry had a chance to prove himself in the eyes of the newspapermen first, and then, in the eyes of the members of the House of Commons.
But he showed us first that the government does not know any more than he does about
Interim Supply
feed grain subsidies and that he relied on trucking competition to get some results from that policy.
During the proceedings of the committee on agriculture and colonization last fall, if my memory serves me right, a member of the official opposition proposed the establishment of an agency in order to study the matter thoroughly and to bring in the required improvements.
In his announcement the minister said that he was waiting for the report of the committee on agriculture and colonization to make a final decision in that respect.
We will wait for a long time, because the matter of feed grain has not yet been referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization during this session.
Once again, we see how sincere is the government about that problem. Considering its attitude, this government does not wish to help farmers. There are fine opportunities and great needs.
I am asking the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry to give their attention to that highly important matter.
I would like in addition to ask the Minister of Forestry and I regret his absence from the house this evening-
He is on a jaunt to Europe.

-because I had several questions to ask him. Anyhow, I should like to know whether as claimed by Mr. Jacques Guay in a magazine article published in Le Magazine Maclean, it is true that the administration of ARDA gives rise to shameful political favouritism in the province of Quebec.
According to Mr. Guay, one cannot work as a settler under ARDA unless one professes to be a partisan of the Liberal party. Allow me to quote one of Mr. Guay's statements as reported in Le Magazine Maclean:
In St. Joachim de Tourelle, I met a young man of eighteen who had to give $2 to the patronage dispenser of the Liberal party-
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm read that this afternoon.
-to manage to get a job on an ARDA project-
This is a repetition.
We have to repeat things to you seven or eight times.

-if you are not taken on, you will get your money back, he was told.

Interim Supply
I want the minister to deny flatly this statement.
He is in Europe.

If this allegation is not founded, the minister should flatly deny that patronage is being dispensed with regard to ARDA, because even though ARDA, which was established by the Conservatives, is administered by the Liberal government in the province of Quebec, the fact remains that the federal government makes its contribution and is therefore authorized to control the actions of the Liberal government of the province of Quebec in this connection.
The minister is on holiday in Europe.
He is on official business.
I should like to direct other questions to the minister, but as he is conspicuous by his absence, having decided to take a vacation, I shall ask them when he is back in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Grey-Bruce.
This should be good.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Well, when you are ready to make your contribution we will be ready to listen to you.
On a point of order, I just want to say I do not intend to interrupt this filibuster.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I am very interested in the views of the hon. member. He says he does not want to participate in this debate. This is precisely what is taking place on the part of those sitting in the front benches on the other side. For a long time during the course of this session we have been waiting to discuss certain phases of government administration. It is my understanding that one of the basic functions of parliament is the discussion of the spending program of the government. Because this discussion has been delayed we feel that it is not only our privilege but our duty to bring these matters to the attention of the country. I have noted in the course of the present session, as a result of one of the small responsibilities which is mine, that the members on this side of the house have done more than their duty with regard to the functioning of the committees of this parliament. They have carried the quorums, I might say, in practically every case.

In the vast majority of cases many of the committees of the house would not have functioned had it not been for the members of the official opposition. This is also one of the responsibilities of the backbenchers and supporters of the government.
Then we come to the situation where my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm puts his finger on the core of the matter relating to the lack of responsibility of the Minister of Forestry and his good wife, and the money which has been taken from the taxpayers of the country and spent as it has been. This matter was discussed today, and the information given must be correct because it has not been refuted. So that when hon. members talk of descending to low levels, when the performance of this party ever stoops as low as the level of performance of hon. members opposite in an election campaign, then that will be the day I will leave this party.
Now, there are some matters of legislation-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member should address the Chair.
He is addressing "Mr. Pigeon."

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I regret causing the Chair any embarrassment in this regard, Mr. Chairman.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there has apparently been some suspicion over the program we have been following, but let me dispel these fears immediately. As I have said, this is one of our basic functions in parliament and we intend to carry it out, as we should, for the benefit of the country and everyone in Canada. Not only that, but we also feel that if the government were responsible they would bring forth the legislation which the people of this country want discussed. It does not take very much to appreciate what these items are. I have mentioned this before in the course of this session and it has borne some fruit at one time or another. But we have reached the stage of obstinacy as far as this government is concerned. If you look down the order paper-

speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) wants to be recognized.
Mr. Chairman, it is any member's privilege to stand up and speak in the house, but I do not wish to interrupt the filibuster; I, therefore, waive this privilege.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that most hon. members in this house might have learned a very important lesson on how the business of the house should be discussed if they had been here and had paid attention to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. The forestry industry in Canada, as he pointed out, is very important. I thought that, having in mind the logical way in which he discussed this subject, the way in which he so clearly illustrated to all of us the many different problems of that industry, the many different ways in which that industry is of prime importance to this country, we would have had more of that same logical type of discussion. Certainly, I feel such remarks as those made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere, who obviously comes from a district that is dependant upon the forest industry, are out of place. He said that he would not take the time of the house to speak on this

Interim Supply
subject. However, when he considered there was a personal affront to him he took the time to get up and call that to the attention of the house. I suggest it behooves the hon. member to put the welfare of his constituents and a very important industry ahead of his own personal feelings. I hope he sends home many copies of Hansard with these great speeches of his tonight, so those people who have some realization of the importance of forestry will know how well he is taking care of their affairs in Ottawa.
It may be that I am not an expert on this subject. I understand that there are members who feel rather reluctant to speak on subjects on which they might not be fully informed. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that if we all sat silent and allowed only the experts to speak on these occasions we would have very little debate and there would be few worth-while ideas brought forward. All of us would I think be properly branded as cowards who had deserted their duty. There is no better way, I believe, of realizing the importance of the forests of this country than to live in it and travel in it from one end to the other.
We have a good deal of forested area in Alberta. We have a wide variety of trees. There is a tremendous difference between the trees we have in Alberta and those in Ontario, for instance. I think that even to travel that distance, to see the different kinds and quantities of lumber, to see the different ways in which trees affect the lives of not only the farmers but of all of us, is to give any person some idea of the enormity of the task to be faced by any department of government which is going to mobilize its resources to give us the fullest possible benefit from this important natural heritage of ours.
I noticed the former minister, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, mentioned forest fires. He referred to the total loss of timber by forest fires and compared it to the total commercial production. It seemed that there was at least two thirds as much destroyed by fire as there was used commercially. When we consider how excited we have become in this house at the threat to even one part of the production of this industry, such as the possible imposition of a tariff by the United States against B.C. lumber, and how concerned we became at the possibility of having that valuable export market made more difficult, and when we realize that export market is only a small part of the total production of the country and is insignificant compared to the amount lost by

fire, and when we consider along with that the amount of money spent on fire protection, then all of us must realize we have a duty to look more closely at the methods of fire prevention. We should all be attempting to bring forward suggestions as to how we might prevent some of this tremendous waste.
I believe it does not do any of us in the house any harm to get up and give a pat on the back to those who are working so hard on research in connection with this serious problem. There are many who have developed, and are still developing, new techniques for fighting forest fires. I refer to the manner in which former military airplanes have been converted into water bombers, for instance; the way in which paratroopers have been trained to become firefighters; the new methods of strategically placing firefighting men and materials, and so on. I feel they all deserve the support of this house. I am sure there is not one member who would like to go back to his constituency and report that a substantial loss of money by theft was occurring in one part of the country or another and that the government had not taken it very seriously. However, when we consider that we have to face the taxpayers of Canada and say that their property, these great forests of ours which have meant so much and will continue to mean so much to Canada, have been harvested to a greater extent by fire than by lumbermen, we should blush just a little.
I know that there is a considerable amount of money being spent on research, and I hope that we will not be niggardly in connection with experiments on firefighting techniques. I have seen some of the fires or seen pictures of some of the fires that have raged in this country. I have wondered at such times if the Department of Forestry could not co-operate with the army a little more so that army personnel could be made available as firefighters. With the airlifting techniques that have been perfected by the air force and the fact that we have many troops who are easily and quickly mobilized, it should not be beyond the realm of practicability to organize firefighting brigades in different parts of the country and to work out arrangements with the civilian authorities to bring in by airlift special companies of troops to assist in areas where a sufficient number of firefighters is not readily available.
In the case of many fires which start to consume a large area and rage out of control it is quite common for the police to stop vehicles on the roads and to press every man

into service for this task. I know that sometimes this causes considerable hardship to some individuals, but they do not really complain about the necessity. Most of them readily understand the value of our forests and the danger to them and other property, as well as the loss of wildlife. Most of them serve as valiantly and effectively as they can, but as in any other endeavour I believe that the presence of trained troops who can be controlled and whose work can be directed would mean that man for man they would be much more effective in firefighting.
I have nothing more to say about forest fires. There are other aspects of the forest industry that I think are equally as important. For instance, there is the question of our national parks. It has been said in the house before that our trees are a recurring resource. Trees can be grown like farm crops. They can be properly cut and harvested under good forest management, and with proper provision for replanting we can always have plenty of trees.
In many of our national parks today there are huge areas of merchantable timber and there are many people anxious to be allowed to cut it. I am aware of course of the tremendous feeling and fear on the part of many people that this would be a desecration of our parks. I concede that where permission is granted for commercial tree cutting or any other commercial venture in our parks, due regard must be had for the preservation of these beauty spots of nature so that all may enjoy them and treasure them for years. But there are out of the way places that are never seen now by tourists. In these areas the trees grow old and die or are destroyed by fires. There are agreas where lumbering could be a fairly profitable industry and the operation could be controlled in such a way that the harm would be negligible. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I think such operations would be beneficial to the parks.
I can recall a recent instance with regard to which I had occasion to speak to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. It involved a very small stretch of timber just within Wood Buffalo park in Alberta. Wood Buffalo park is the largest of our national parks. The area is tremendous and it is visited by very few people. There is a great deal of timber and there are small timber operations there now.
Where is that?

Wood Buffalo park is in Alberta and the Northwest Territories and its
Interim Supply
size is tremendous. I know that the people concerned had a problem. They wanted to cut timber along the edge of the park. I had occasion to speak to the minister about the matter. I might say that I feared I would encounter the attitude usually displayed by officialdom. When people want to put a finger on the parks they say: No, they are sacred; you cannot touch them.
I found the minister to be most reasonable in his approach. He pointed out to me some of the difficulties, including the fact that the province of Alberta would like to have some of this parkland. This would require some consultation with the province, because if there was going to be any exchange of land the minister would not want to impose on the province responsibility for any industry that might be operating there at the time.
I mention this only because I think it illustrates in a small way, though I think a rather important one, that our ideas with regard to our forests in our national parks do not have to be firm, fixed and inflexible. Through proper negotiation with the provinces and the federal officials we can work out reasonable methods by which these tremendous forest resources can be usefully employed to furnish greater wealth for this country. I hope the minister will see that many more officials of his department look at our national parks to ascertain where good timber cutting can be done with beneficial effects. I hope that many officials of the Department of Forestry will also study more carefully the accessibility and availability of timber, and that the roads to resources program started by the previous government will be extended and expanded. I trust that every facility will be made available to private enterprise which shows a sense of responsibility, some ambition and some knowledge of the timber industry.
We are well aware in Canada today of the necessity for expanding our export markets and earning dollars wherever we can. We hear many members speak about the unemployment in their own ridings, and in view of the history of employment and good business operations in the timber industry there is no reason, despite our difficulties in other more highly mechanized or automated industries, why the tried and true methods of garnering the wealth of our greatest national resource, our forests, should lag behind. I hope that the availability of timber will be a subject of research.

INDUSTRY-TIMMINS    PROCESSING OF ORE FROM NEW MINING DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the right hon. Prime Minister is unable to be in the house tonight because the question that I raised the other day, and which I am raising again tonight, is one of vital importance not only to the people of my constituency but to the people of the north country as a whole. It has to do with the arrangements that are reputedly being made about the smelter that will deal with the ores found in Timmins this spring.
Hon. members may recall that some weeks ago I raised this matter when the suggestion at that time was that the smelter would be built in North Carolina, and possibly as a result of the representations I made then an announcement was forthcoming that the smelter would be built in Canada, and more particularly in Ontario. Since then it appears
[Mr. Choquette.l

everybody has been trying to get into the act and everybody wants the Timmins smelter.
For example it has been reported that it would be built at Parry Sound on Georgian bay. When that report came out the people of the north country got very suspicious, because of a certain connection. The member of the provincial legislature for that constituency also happens to be commissioner of the Ontario Northland Railway which would be involved in any agreement to ship this ore. Also the suspicion was raised that there were possible political connotations to this matter.
Now we have been informed by a reasonably reliable authority that Cutler, in Algoma East riding, is talked about as the prospective site for this smelter. Again to the people of northern Ontario, this would smack of political interference and political pressure in regard to the location of the smelter.
It is economically ridiculous to ship ore, such as will be produced at the Texas Gulf strike in Timmins, over long distance by rail or by road. Zinc, even in the concentrated form, still represents about 50 per cent waste, and copper some 66 per cent waste. This would mean that they would be paying freight on 50 per cent waste in one instance and 66 per cent waste in the other, which makes no economic sense whatever. This leads the people of the north country to believe that there must be some other factor involved in this hesitation on the part of officials to announce that the smelter will be built at the place where it should be built, which is in the Timmins area.
The freight policy of our railways is that they offer a very cheap rate for unfinished products and charge a very high rate for finished products. Again the people of northern Ontario feel this is doing nothing more than turning it into a raw material economic colony for the people of the south. The treasure we have in northern Ontario is mined in its raw form, which provides very little employment. In fact the ratio of employment is about three times greater in the smelting work than in mining the ore.
Mr. Speaker, something came to my attention very recently which is of great importance here. I would like to show that this is not only a provincial problem solely under the jurisdiction of the province. On Sunday night there was an excellent program broadcast over the Timmins t.v. station, dealing with the Grand canal project. I think most hon. members are familiar with this project. It is a plan that is apparently coming to the

point of utter necessity by which fresh waters flowing north into James bay can be reversed and sent back over land heights, to maintain the level of water in the great lakes and in the St. Lawrence system. I think all hon. members are beginning to realize how desperate this water situation is becoming in the whole of the great lakes basin and the St. Lawrence seaway. There is a double problem here. One is to maintain the level of water in the lakes and the other is maintain a flow through the system which would keep shipping moving through the seaway.
It seems to me it is ridiculous to aggravate an already critical situation in the south by establishing industries there which could be built in the north. I think the government should be adopting the idea of moving industries up north so that they could take advantage of the natural flow of waters to the north which remains unharnessed at the present time. This is something the federal government is bound to be involved in, because this new Grand canal project is not only an interprovincial one; it is also an international one which can only be handled in all its aspects by the federal government. It is something which will come about very rapidly and which will call for the attention of this house and of the government.
Not only do we ship our raw materials down from the north at the present time but we find we have to ship the water out afterwards in order to process it. I think this is a senseless procedure and the stated policy of governments, whether federal or provincial, should be to rectify this situation. I should like an assurance from the Prime Min-

Though it may be considered to be in northern Ontario, Cutler is still on the south slope, because the slope of the land comes close to Timmins and Kirkland Lake. All water to the south flows into the St. Lawrence basin, and the arguments I have put forward apply. As I say, I should like an assurance from the Prime Minister or his parliamentary secretary that no such plans are on foot at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: INDUSTRY-TIMMINS    PROCESSING OF ORE FROM NEW MINING DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I should like to thank the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) for making such a persuasive case for locating more industry up north. Certainly he has made a strong case for locating a smelter in the Timmins area. His original question asked, in effect, what submissions the Prime Minister had received in this connection. My right hon. friend has received several oral submissions, one from the mayor of Little Current, one from the improvement district of Elliot Lake and one from the residents along the north short of lake Huron in the vicinity of Cutler, Ontario.
These people have all been anxious to point out the advantages of locating a smelter on, or close to, water transportation. No doubt the mining companies will take this and other important considerations into account and will certainly locate a smelter in Canada having regard to these possibilities.
